title: Akins sworn in as new commissioner
description: Mickey Starling reporter3@greenepublishing.com The Madison City Commission held a special meeting on Tuesday, June 18, to address the need of filling the District Three seat vacated by Larry Olive…
content:
Mickey Starling
reporter3@greenepublishing.com
The Madison City Commission held a special meeting on Tuesday, June 18, to address the need of filling the District Three seat vacated by Larry Olive, who relocated to Texas. The position needed to be filled by Wednesday, June 26. Otherwise, Gov. Ron DeSantis would select a replacement. Only one person was present who expressed interest in joining the commission. Priscilla Akins introduced herself to the commissioners, saying, 'I am a lifelong resident of Madison, and I am very interested in being a part of this team.'
Commissioner Voncyle Wilson made a motion in favor of Akins becoming the District Three commissioner, and Mayor Judy Townsend passed the gavel to Commissioner Byron Poore in order to second the motion. Akins received a unanimous 4-0 vote to join the Madison City Commission. She will have to run for election in March of 2026 and again in 2028 since she joined the board by appointment. Akins was immediately sworn into office by Attorney Tom Reeves.

title: Boyz to Kings holds awards ceremony
description: Mickey Starling reporter3@greenepublishing.com A large crowd gathered on Tuesday, May 28, for the Boyz to Kings (BTK) Awards Day, held in the James Madison Preparatory High School gym. Many hard-w…
content:
Mickey Starling
reporter3@greenepublishing.com
A large crowd gathered on Tuesday, May 28, for the Boyz to Kings (BTK) Awards Day, held in the James Madison Preparatory High School gym. Many hard-working students were honored during the ceremony in a variety of ways, including A-B Honor Rolls, Study Hall Awards, No Referrals Awards and the Elmer Spears Award.
The event was opened in prayer by Jordan Capi, followed by Boyz to Kings Youth President Avery Brinson, who welcomed everyone to the festivities. BTK Founder Merv Mattair then introduced BTK team members, board members and alumni. He went on to introduce the guest speaker for the evening, BTK Alumni Zion Lamar, who is presently attending North Carolina Wesleyan University. He stressed the need for determination and diligence in pursuing your goals and having the support of great mentors.
The presentation of awards followed, With Mattair beginning by recognizing BTK members who made the A or B Honor Roll. Those students making the B Honor Roll were: Ahmir Dye, Jayden McQuay, Jayceon Gallon, Kaiden Craddock, Quintavious Norwood, Jatavion Mobley, Keonate Mattair, Avery Brinson, Michael Pride, Jaiden Johnson, Devonte Williams, Tyrik Tillman, Zamarion West, Dertez Lamar and Kevin Gilley. A Honor Roll recipients were: Da'Quarious Gibson, Amiylon Roberson, Jayceon Robinson, Legend Gilliard, Xavier Richardson, Kai Herbin, Ma'khi Ghent, Kaden Ruth, Brycen Ware, Christon Wright, Quincy Barfield, Ke'Andre Dobson, TJ Mattair and King Chandler.
Next, Vickie Donaldson and Julie Pries teamed up to present the Study Hall Awards. Those recognized were: Joshua Stawder, Most Diligent; Jayden Weatherspoon, Most Improved Middle School; Legend Gilliard, Most Diligent; DeAndre Strawder, Most Improved; Dan Gibson, Most Enthusiastic Towards Learning; Jayceon Gallon, who also received a special award from Pries.
Then, Curtis Mattair and Bobby Thompkins presided over the special individual awards. The two recipients for the Leadership Award were Avery Brinson and Elijah McNealy. Jordan Capi won the Extra Mile Award and Martevious Ghent took home the Most Impressionable Award.
In the largest category of winners, the threesome of Vickie Donaldson, Bobby Thompkins and Shirley Mattair presented the No Referrals Award. These students kept a clean record, making no trips to the principal's office, other than to offer pleasantries and tend to school business. These well-behaved young scholars were: Devontae Williams, Torey Damon, Za'Marion West, Kai Herbin, Ezekiel Ghent, Jaiden Shannon, Di'Kwez Akins, Quincy Barfield, Elijah McNealy, Amarion Bunion, Javis Mcgahee, Jayden McQuay, TJ Mattair, Keonate Mattair, Auntra Lamar, Qintavious Norwood, Legend Gilliard, Xavier Richardson, Jatavion Mobley, Taevon Bonds, Micah Thompkins, Josiah Robinson, Jaclyn Robinson, Railey Montgomery, Travis, Gallon, Tory Damon and Brycen Ware.
The final offering of the night was the Elmer Spears Award, with two worthy students receiving a trophy and $100 each. Merv and Denise Mattair partnered with Greg Turner in presenting Keondre Dobson and TJ Mattair with their awards.
Another special treat for the evening occurred when Peter Walley, who is a model-airplane enthusiast, donated a P-51 Mustang replica to Boyz to Kings. The planes were made famous by the Tuskegee Airmen, who flew and fought with great success during World War II.
The ceremonies ended with remarks by BTK Mentor of the Year Greg Turner and the Boyz to Kings chant, led by Maliki Gibson and the BTK youth.

content:

Tri-County Electric Cooperative (TCEC) recently awarded ten James Madison Preparatory High School (JMPHS) students with the TCEC Energizing Education Scholarship.
This year, TCEC awarded $43,000 in scholarships to 23 students in Madison, Jefferson and Taylor Counties. This investment in the future leaders of the communities TCEC serves was made possible through their Energizing Education program, with TCEC Members rounding up their electric statement to the next dollar and giving those cents to the TCEC Energizing Scholarship fund.
The following students received the TCEC Energizing Education Scholarship: Abigail Saltares, Addison Jacobs, Anna Meyer, Blake Grass, Callie Knight, Gracie Jenkins, Jailyn Cooks, Josie Driggers, Lillian Washington and Roxanne Gosseck.
Congratulations to all the recipients!
To enroll your TCEC account, visit www.tcec.com/energizing-education.

title: More improvements ahead for Camp Cherry Lake
description: Rick Patrick rick@greenepublishing.com During an open meeting on Friday, June 21, several members of the community learned of more big plans for the 4-H camp at Cherry Lake, in Madison County. Tha…
content:
Rick Patrick
rick@greenepublishing.com
During an open meeting on Friday, June 21, several members of the community learned of more big plans for the 4-H camp at Cherry Lake, in Madison County. Thanks to a generous $1.1 million United States Department of Agriculture Rural Development Grant, plans are under way for a new, multi-purpose building to hold an auditorium and classrooms. This will greatly enhance the educational programs offered by the youth development program of the University of Florida Institute of Food and Agricultural Sciences (UF/IFAS). Through their extension service, UF/IFAS administers the 4-H program throughout the state. The building will also be available for use by community groups to hold conferences, meetings, etc. Funds have been set aside for the project, and UF/IFAS is in the process of completing the requirements for the grant. Groundbreaking on the new multi-purpose building is expected to take place in 2026.
Dating back to 1937, Camp Cherry Lake is one of three camps still operating in the state. Over the decades, generations of young people have developed leadership skills, experienced hands-on outdoor learning and have made life-long friends through participation in summer camps at Camp Cherry Lake. There is a separate campaign ongoing for the construction of five new, modern cabins to replace the old, primitive cabins which were previously used. So far, approximately $255,000 has been received through private donations to go along with $900,000 in state funding recently approved by Governor Ron DeSantis. Plans are underway to request another $10.6 million in funding from the state legislature.
To help support Camp Cherry Lake, or for more information, please contact Caylin Hilton, Director of Development at (352) 392-5432, or by email at grow4H@ifas.ufl.edu. You may also contact Stacey Ellison, PhD, 4-H State Program Leader at (352) 846-4444, or by email at staceye@ufl.edu. Locally, the Madison County 4H Coordinator, Beth Moore, can be reached at (850) 973-4138, or by email at elizabethmoore@ufl.edu.

The students also attended classes and seminars aimed at promoting patriotism in their communities. A special highlight of the trip was an in-person appearance and address from President Donald Trump.

'We're not a political group, not technically,' said Vickers. 'People liked to call us the 'Republican Club,' simply because of how patriotic we are, which is exactly what everyone should be in our country.'

title: Lawsuit filed in Clerk of Courts race
description: Rick Patrick rick@greenepublishing.com Current Madison County Clerk of Courts Billy Washington has filed suit, alleging his challenger, Beulah Farquharson, failed to properly qualify for the upcom…
content:
Rick Patrick
rick@greenepublishing.com
Current Madison County Clerk of Courts Billy Washington has filed suit, alleging his challenger, Beulah Farquharson, failed to properly qualify for the upcoming November election. In his suit, Washington makes the claim that the Clerk of Courts and Comptroller for Madison County office is a partisan office and, therefore, would require a candidate to declare a political party.
Florida Statute 99.021 requires candidates to declare that they have been a member of the political party for which they are seeking a nomination for at least 365 days prior to qualifying. If the candidate is claiming 'no party affiliation,' they must not have been a member of any political party for the 365 days prior to qualifying. According to the court records in Washington's suit, Farquharson changed her party affiliation from 'no party affiliation (NPA)' to 'democrat' on May 7, 2024, when she completed her voter registration. According to Madison County Supervisor of Elections, Heath Driggers, the Clerk of Courts is a partisan office, but NPA candidates may run.
When Farquharson signed her oath stating she was a member of the democrat party, she added several asterisks on her 'Statement of Party' and added her own hand written statement, stating, 'Signed under protest. The 365 days violates my State and Federal Constitutional rights.' Washington's suit claims the addition of the asterisks and her hand written addition to the oath, 'unlawfully altered the language required by Florida Statutes 99.061(7)(a)(3) and 99.021(1)(b) and Rule 1S-2.001, Florida Administrative Code.'
Washington's suit claims that 'Washington has a clear legal right to appear on the ballot without Farquharson as a competing candidate … Washington will suffer irreparable harm should Farquharson be permitted to be on the ballot in multiple ways: a) Washington's right to run for election against only those candidates who are legally qualified to run for the office of Clerk of the Courts and Comptroller for Madison County, Florida will be extinguished. b) The public will incorrectly think there is an alternatively legally qualified candidate for the office of Clerk of the Courts and Comptroller for Madison County, Florida. c) Washington will have to devote time, money and other resources to running for office against a candidate who has not legally qualified for election. d) As the current Clerk of the Courts and Comptroller for Madison County, Florida, should Washington lose the election to Farquharson, he will have lost his office to a candidate who is not legally qualified for election in the first place.'
Greene Publishing, Inc. reached out to Farquharson for a comment. 'My response to u [sic] will be my reply to the lawsuit after I am served, other than nothing alleged against me in Washington [sic] lawsuit is factual, and it spouts half truths with twisted innuendos to sound unlawful but is not,' said Farquharson in an email response. 'Washington and his Attorneys are grasping for straws to keep a bad clerk of court elected without having to run a campaign for the seat, for if it wasn't for me entering the race, the incompetent incumbent would have just won 4 more years undeservingly.'
In her Candidate Oath, dated Friday, June 14, Farquharson claimed she was 'now homeless in Madison County.' Driggers stated Farquharson was allowed to use the Supervisor of Elections office address as her residential address in order to be assigned to a precinct.
This is not the first time Farquharson has attempted to run for office. She previously ran for Osceola County, Fla. Supervisor of Elections in 2020, where she was defeated by the incumbent, 76 percent to 24 percent of the vote. She also ran for Ocseola County Commission in 2022, a race in which her opponent earned 73 percent of the vote. In 2006, she and ran for Florida House of Representatives for District 79, and was defeated by Republican Frank Attkisson, 64.8 percent to 35.2 percent. She was ordered by the Florida Elections Commission to pay a fine of $337.50, in 2016 for failing to file a campaign treasurer's report and pay a subsequently assessed fine.
The General Election is scheduled for Tuesday, Nov. 5.

title: A hero comes home
description: Rick Patrick rick@greenepublishing.com On the morning of Thursday, July 11, law enforcement officers from Madison County, and throughout North Central Florida honored a fallen hero as the ashes of…
content:
Rick Patrick
rick@greenepublishing.com
On the morning of Thursday, July 11, law enforcement officers from Madison County, and throughout North Central Florida honored a fallen hero as the ashes of Madison County Sheriff's Office (MCSO) K9 Archer were brought home. Archer tragically passed away from a heat stroke after helping to apprehend a fleeing criminal on Thursday, July 4.
As soon as Archer began to show signs of distress, he was taken to Madison Veterinary Clinic. Archer was later transported to Allied Veterinary Care, in Tallahassee, before being taken to the University of Florida Small Animal Hospital, considered by many to be one of the best veterinary hospitals in the region. Despite their efforts, Archer passed away on Friday, July 5.
After he was cremated, Archer's ashes were transported back to Madison with an escort consisting of law enforcement agencies from across the region. An emotional Madison County Sheriff David Harper expressed his gratitude for the prayers and the outpouring of love and support his agency has received from across the state and the nation.
Archer was six years old and had been serving Madison County for approximately five years.
A memorial service for K9 Archer will be held on Thursday, July 18, at 10:30 a.m. The service will take place at Madison County High School (MCHS). Dignitaries are asked to contact MCSO Undersheriff Chris Andrews, at (850) 251-0416, in order to reserve seating. Doors will open at 10 a.m.

title: Decision made on school consolidation
description: Rick Patrick rick@greenepublishing.com During the regular meeting of the Madison County District School Board, on Monday, July 15, Board Member Katie Knight stated this was a decision the current …
content:
Rick Patrick
rick@greenepublishing.com
During the regular meeting of the Madison County District School Board, on Monday, July 15, Board Member Katie Knight stated this was a decision the current board should not have to make. In her eyes, the decision should have been made years before. That decision being what to do about the outlying elementary schools of Greenville, Lee and Pinetta,in the face of decreasing student population.
Much of the funding for the school system comes from the State of Florida, and that funding is based on the number of students enrolled and attending school in the district. Enrollment numbers in the public school system in Madison County has been declining for many years. There could be several contributing factors for this, such as fewer families with school-age children moving in, a lack of industry in the county to attract families, and students going to charter schools, private schools, other school districts, etc. With fewer students in the schools, fewer dollars were coming from Tallahassee. Estimates are, that trend is likely to continue into the future.
After several months of discussion and town hall-style meetings, it was becoming clear to some on the board that something would need to be done. There were those who were strongly in favor of 'keeping their small community schools.' Others felt more discussion and more options still needed to be explored. On the other hand, some felt 'the can had been kicked down the road' too many times, and it was time to make a difficult decision. 'We cannot stall any longer,' said Superintendent of Schools, Shirley Joseph.
'We should be committed to every child, not just one school,' added Board Member Katie Knight.
In her recommendations to the board, which Supt. Joseph stated were completely 'data driven,' and not based on any political pressure or any sense of loyalty to any one community, she suggested the following:
• Consolidate any school that has less than 250 students enrolled. It was stated that this is 'the number of students needed to generate enough state funding to effectively support operations of a school. This would include Greenville, Lee and Pinetta Elementary Schools.
• Move all district public PreK through sixth grade students to Madison County Central School (MCCS).
• Move all district traditional public school grade seven and eight students to Madison County High School (MCHS).
A motion was made and seconded to accept the recommendations. Board Member Devin Thompson expressed reservations about the seventh and eighth grade students moving to MCHS. The motion was amended to include only the consolidation of any school that has less than 250 students enrolled. After more discussion, a vote was taken and the motion passed with a 3-2 vote. Board Members VeEtta Hagan and Carol Gibson cast the dissenting votes.
The decision will take effect with the 2025-2026 school year. Board Member Thompson stated her desire to immediately form committees, taken from members of the community, county and civic leaders, representatives from North Florida College, parents and other interested parties to formulate plans on how best to implement the school consolidation. This includes what is best to do with the physical locations and buildings of Greenville, Lee and Pinetta Elementary Schools.
There will be a special meeting of the Madison County District School Board on Monday, July 22, starting at 6 p.m. The meeting is set to take place in the Board Meeting Room, located at 210 NE Duval Ave., in Madison.

title: Lawyers association regional chapter opens second annual teacher giveaway
description: Kenzie James news@greenepublishing.com The third judicial circuit chapter for the Florida Association of Women Lawyers (FAWL) announced earlier this month they are accepting teacher nominations fo…
content:
Kenzie James
news@greenepublishing.com
The third judicial circuit chapter for the Florida Association of Women Lawyers (FAWL) announced earlier this month they are accepting teacher nominations for their second annual classroom wish list giveaway, and the nomination period ends next week.
FAWL's third circuit chapter announced on Tuesday, July 9 that they will pick a teacher from the nominees and fulfill their classroom wish list for the upcoming school year. Nominated teachers must be from one of the following counties in the third judicial circuit: Columbia, Dixie, Hamilton, Lafayette, Madison, Suwannee or Taylor.
Kylie Kafka, president of the FAWL third circuit chapter, said the chapter started the back-to-school giveaway last year, to give back to the community and highlight local educators. The chapter is a donation-based organization, and Kafka shared they are grateful for the donations from businesses, sponsors and community members they received last year to help them achieve their goal for the giveaway and fulfill the winner's wishlist up to $500.
'When we ended the nomination period, we [had] over 130 applicants, and it was too hard to choose just one because every single teacher nominated was so deserving,' Kafka said. 'We put all the names in a random generator, and that is how we picked the winner because, again, every single nominee was deserving and we wanted to be fair to everyone.'
After the wish list teacher was chosen, the chapter's board divided nominees by county and read each nomination, choosing one teacher per county to recognize on Facebook. Kafka said the posts also included the teacher's wish list, and why they were nominated, in an effort to encourage community members to donate.
'We really enjoyed this last year, and we will be doing the same thing this year,' Kafka said. She also wanted to acknowledge the chapter's other board members who help her run the organization: vice president Heidi Kemph, state representative Dana Taylor, treasurer Donna MacRae, secretary Elise Yates and community outreach and social media director Taylor Cheek.
The chapter included a Google Forms link in the Facebook posts for this year's nominations so community members can provide the contact information for the teacher they are nominating, and what makes their favorite teacher the best. Nominations are due on Wednesday, July 23, at 5 p.m. and the winner will be announced on the chapter's Facebook and Instagram pages on Thursday, July 24. The winner's classroom wishlist will be fulfilled, up to $500.

title: Operation Dry Water results released
description: Rick Patrick rick@greenepublishing.com During the recent Fourth of July weekend, the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission (FWC) Division of Law Enforcement (DLE), along with other law…
content:
Rick Patrick
rick@greenepublishing.com
During the recent Fourth of July weekend, the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission (FWC) Division of Law Enforcement (DLE), along with other law enforcement agencies, heightened enforcement as part of 'Operation Dry Water.' Operation Dry Water is a year-round program, designed to educate boaters on the dangers of boating under the influence (BUI) of alcohol; with the hopes of reducing the number of alcohol and drug-related incidents and fatalities on Florida's waterways.
The officers of the North Central Region of the FWC DLE proactively sent boating safety messages to the public prior to the holiday weekend, and continued throughout the weekend, while on the lookout for dangerous or possibly impaired boaters. The North Central Region consists of 17 counties across much of North Florida, from Taylor County, south to Citrus County on the west coast and over to Nassau and Duval Counties to the east. The region includes Hamilton, Lafayette, Madison and Suwannee Counties.
According to a press release from the FWC, from Thursday, July 4, through Sunday, July 7, officers in the region cited 206 vessel operators for boating safety violations, issued 1,119 boating safety warnings and removed six vessel operators from the water due to BUI. The highest blood alcohol content reported was .15. In the Sunshine State, the legal blood alcohol content limit is .08, the same as a land-based motor vehicle. Statewide, over 50 vessel operators were removed from Florida waterways for BUI during the heightened enforcement of the holiday weekend.
'Boating activity, as well as alcohol consumption, is known to increase across the state over the Fourth of July holiday weekend, said Maj. Scott Lee, North Central Florida's Regional Commander. 'Our officers are proud to partner with Operation Dry Water in educating the boating public about the importance of remaining sober while operating a vessel. Their primary goal when they are out there, putting in long hours patrolling and enforcing, is to ensure residents and visitors boat safely.'
The FWC reminds everyone to enjoy their time and the company of friends and family, but to please do it safely. Designate a sober operator before departing from the dock. More information about safe boating can be found at myfwc.com/boating. Information about Operation Dry Water can be found at operationdrywater.org.
To report dangerous boating activity, you can submit an anonymous tip by texting 847411 (Tip411) with the keyword 'FWC,' followed by the location and any information about the violation. You may also call (888) 404-FWCC (3922). There is also an easy-to-use downloadable iPhone or Android app: 'FWC Wildlife Alert.'

title: Learning across history
description: Hailey Heseltine news@greenepublishing.com August has just begun, and now, it's a time known to Florida residents as the peak of the back-to-school season. With less than two weeks until sch…
content:
Hailey Heseltine
news@greenepublishing.com
August has just begun, and now, it's a time known to Florida residents as the peak of the back-to-school season. With less than two weeks until school starts in most of the state's counties, school is on many people's minds.
The history of education is a rich one; institutions of learning have existed for thousands of years. Ancient societies in Egypt, Mesopotamia, China and many other places recognized a need for an education dedicated to the development of literacy, culture and thought. Literacy was seen as a particularly important skill, as those who possessed it could serve important roles in society, such as as scribes.
It is in human nature to learn and teach, and that was seen even when there were not formal schools—at least not in the form we think of them today. In America, education systems were found in Native American tribes. Education was primarily accomplished orally, as the more-experienced ones would teach the younger members of the tribe. Important skills, such as hunting or weaving, were taught through experience. Native American children also learned about history, culture, tradition and even learned to speak some languages of other tribes.
Prior to the creation of public schools in the United States, it was never a guarantee that a child would be able to get an education—whether or not they were able to depended heavily on factors such as economic class, location, race and gender, among others. Schools certainly existed during the colonial times, but they were not nearly as accessible as they were in later centuries. Children depended on parents to teach them all the skills they knew. However, it is important to note that, prior to the wide availability of schools, children were not completely uneducated. Puritan society placed a heavy emphasis on the development of literacy, so many children in the colonies at least knew how to read and write. Besides, if the family were wealthy, children could have private tutors, or they could send their children abroad to attend boarding schools. Churches also sponsored schools, and communities would band together to fund education for their children. The few schools that existed were often founded by parents and operated off of funds earned from tuition. In all, education was not complete inaccessible. Still, there were many children who did not get the opportunity to have a formal education, especially since teachers were short in supply.
The United States' first formal public school, the Boston Latin School, was founded in 1635. It was a boys-only institution that provided an education in the Latin language, which was essential for any student who hoped to attend college. Similar schools sprang up around New England in the years to follow, but they were by no means numerous.
By the time of the American Revolution, many communities had publicly-funded or even free schools for their children. During the 1780s, things began to shift further in favor of education. The new United States' federal government recognized a need for a higher standard of education, and federal land grants began to include the condition that some of the land be used for the building of public schools. This further promoted the development of schools.
It was during the 19th century that education in the United States took a form more similar to the one we see today.
'Normal schools,' schools for educating future teachers, began to be established in the states during the 19th century. The Colombian School in Concord, Vermont, was the first normal school in the United States; it was founded in 1823. It was a private school, but it marked a change. There had long been a shortage of teachers, and the ones who were available were not always educated themselves. The development of normal schools was the solution to this problem.
Horace Mann, a Massachusetts legislator during the 1830s, contributed largely to the development of the modern school system. He advocated for the institution of public normal schools, as he believed that raising the standard of education for teachers would also raise the standard of education for the children. Most importantly, he believed in public, state-funded, widely-available schools for children. These schools would teach skills in literature, arithmetic, history, rhetoric and more. He believed that education for children was essential to the making of productive and morally-upright citizens, which led him to advocate for the cause—and to encourage others to advocate alongside him. Of course, some opposed his ideas, but they mostly were met with approval. Mann's idea of 'common schools' spread far beyond just Massachusetts, and recognized by many to be the creator of the American public school system. By the latter 19th century, about 78 percent of American children were enrolled in public schools. It was then that the classic image of the one-room, quaint little schoolhouse with a stove in the middle became reality for many American children.
Of course, it is important to note that not everyone had the privilege of an education by the turn of the 20th century. Non-white children were not always given the opportunity to go to school, as many had to work or were turned away. The ones who did have the chance to get a formal education were in segregated schools. White children were given the highest standard of learning, and others often had to deal with the pains that came with being in under-funded and under-staffed institutions. These struggles were especially prevalent in the rural south. During these times, communities banded together. Classes were held in houses and churches. Teachers, or even just well-educated ordinary residents, would donate their time to teach children or adults who never had the opportunity to go to school. The education system was unfair, but many resourceful people were willing to learn and share what they learned with others.
Throughout the centuries, many Native American children were taken away from their families and forcibly placed in boarding schools. The schools were often federally-funded, and they were meant to distance the children from their own cultures and to assimilate them into the society created by colonization. Children were often subject to cruelty at these institutions. They were not so much institutions of education as they were institutions of forced assimilation.
Immigrant children were often expected to give up their culture when they attended public schools, including by Americanizing their names and being discouraged from using their native languages; discrimination against immigrants flourished during wave of immigration at the late 19th and early 20th centuries, and it certainly affected the students' quality of schooling.
That is not to mention the quality of education for girls in general, which consistently lagged behind the quality and extent that was available for boys. Even after public schools were successfully established in most states, it still took years for the quality of education available for minorities to catch up.
The development of a public education system has by no means been a smooth process. The education system available to children today is the most widespread it has ever been, and now, most children in the United States are able to get an education. Good education is a need, but it is also a privilege when it is compared to its lack of availability in past times. Going forward into the new school year—either as a parent or as a child—with that sense of thankfulness for the education available today may be just the thing to make this time of year feel a little less daunting.

title: Boil water notice given

Rick Patrick

Because of flooding concerns in some parts of Madison County, some residents are being urged to boil water used for drinking, cooking, etc. The notice comes out of a concern that contaminated flood waters could make their way into the wells of residents living in flooded areas.
Residents who live in the southeastern portion of the county, southeast of Interstate 10 (I-10) and County Road 360, especially in the vicinity of I-10 at exit 258 and were impacted by flood waters are under a boil water notice. This includes those who are under a flood warning or have flood waters on their sewer or well. It is advised that well water used for drinking, cooking, making ice, brushing teeth or washing dishes be boiled. A rolling boiling of one minute should be sufficient. As an alternative, bottled water can also be used. This notice remains in effect until flood waters have receded and well water testing shows the water is safe to drink.
If you are unable to boil water you can disinfect it by adding 1/8 teaspoon (approximately eight drops) of unscented bleach to one gallon of water. Mix well and wait 30 minutes before drinking.

title: Private Well Water sample collection instructions to follow
description: Leah Androski reporter@greenepublishing.com Bacteriological Water Sample (Bac-T) 1. Wear gloves when collecting samples, if possible. 2. Remove attachments from tap. Remove aerator, hose, strainer …
content:
Leah Androski
reporter@greenepublishing.com
Bacteriological Water Sample (Bac-T)
1. Wear gloves when collecting samples, if possible.
2. Remove attachments from tap. Remove aerator, hose, strainer or any items attached to faucet.
3. Clean faucet with bleach solution (one tsp. bleach per quart of water) or clean faucet with 70 percent isopropyl alcohol.
4. Allow the water from the faucet and well to run a minimum of five minutes at full flow before sampling.
5. Close faucet to a stream of water the size of a pencil.
6. Remove lid from the sample container. If the lid unscrews, make sure to hold it by the edges with the bottom facing downwards.
7. Do not rinse out the bottle. Do not allow the chlorine neutralizer (white dust) to fall out of the container or be rinsed out.
8. Carefully fill sample container with cold water to the 100mL mark, located on the side of the sample container. Do not touch the lip or inside of the sterile container with anything but the clean catch water sample. Do not overflow.
9. It is best if one sample is taken outside the house close to the well. The other sample from in the home either the bathroom or kitchen sink.
10. After sampling, place lid on the sample container carefully and tighten.
11. Write the system name of the 'top' of the sample container. Mark sample container as to where the sample was taken, i.e., well, bathroom, kitchen.
12. You must preserve the sample on ice, or your sample will not be accepted.
13. Bring sample to the Health Department in Madison County before 12:30 p.m., Monday through Thursday, the same day you collected the sample.

title: Preparing your pets for disasters
description: Leah Androski reporter@greenepublishing.com As we continue through hurricane season, it is a good idea to have an emergency plan in place. Emergency planning with your family should include your pe…
content:
Leah Androski
reporter@greenepublishing.com
As we continue through hurricane season, it is a good idea to have an emergency plan in place. Emergency planning with your family should include your pets as well. Here are some tips to ensure that your family is prepared for a disaster:
Make a Plan. When you make a plan, you are more likely to experience less difficulty, stress and worry when making a decision during the emergency. This should include having an evacuation plan for your pet(s), developing a buddy system, having copies of your pet's vaccination record, making sure your pet is microchipped and keeping contact information for local emergency management office or animal control office and shelters in case you are separated from your pet.
Build a Kit for your Pet. Your kit can include: food (in an airtight, waterproof container), water (have a water bowl ready to use), medicine (keep in waterproof container), first aid kit, backup collar with ID tag and harness or leash (it is recommended to have copies of your pet's registration information in a waterproof container and available electronically), traveling bag, crate or sturdy carrier for each pet, grooming items (pet shampoo, brushes, etc.), a picture of you and your pet together (in case you are separated), sanitation needs and familiar items.
Stay Informed. Stay informed of current conditions. Download the FEMA app to receive weather alerts for up to five different locations anywhere in the United States.
Always bring your pets inside at the first sign or warning of a storm. For more information, visit Ready.gov/pets.

title: Heart disease statistics
description: Leah Androski reporter@greenepublishing.com The leading cause of deaths globally are Cardiovascular Diseases (CVDs), which take around 17.9 million lives yearly. CVDs are compiled of a group of dis…
content:
Leah Androski
reporter@greenepublishing.com
The leading cause of deaths globally are Cardiovascular Diseases (CVDs), which take around 17.9 million lives yearly. CVDs are compiled of a group of disorders of the heart and blood vessels, which can include: Coronary Heart Disease, Cerebrovascular Disease, Rheumatic Heart Disease and many other conditions. Four out of five CVD deaths are due to heart attacks and strokes, and one third of those deaths occur prematurely in people under 70 years old.
In the U.S., one person dies every 33 seconds from a cardiovascular disease. The most common heart disease is Coronary Artery Disease (CAD). In the U.S., about one in 20 adults aged 20 years and older have CAD. In 2022, in the U.S., about one out of five deaths from cardiovascular disease was among adults younger than 65-years-old. CAD can be screened, identified and treated early if caught.
In the U.S., heart attacks happen every 40 seconds. Every year in the U.S., around 805,000 people have a heart attack. 605,000 are first heart attacks, and 200,000 are people who have already had a heart attack before. About one in five heart attacks are silent. Early action is important for a heart attack. Symptoms of a heart attack can include: chest pain or discomfort, feeling weak, light-headed, faint, pain or discomfort in the jaw, neck, back, in one or both arms, shoulders and/or shortness of breath. Other symptoms, mostly for women, can include: unusual or unexplained tiredness, nausea or vomiting.
Risk factors for heart disease and stroke are an unhealthy diet, tobacco use, physical inactivity and harmful use of alcohol. Air pollution can also play an important factor, as well. High blood pressure, high blood cholesterol and smoking are also other key factors for developing heart disease.
Stopping tobacco use, reducing salt in the diet, eating more fruit and vegetables, regular physical activity and avoiding harmful use of alcohol have been shown to reduce the risk of cardiovascular disease.
For more information, please visit the CDC's website at cdc.gov/heart-disease/data-research/facts-stats/index/html.

title: NAIM brings vaccine awareness
description: Leah Androski reporter@greenepublishing.com August is National Immunization Awareness Month (NIAM). NIAM raises awareness about why vaccines are important for people of all ages, and how they can p…
content:
Leah Androski
reporter@greenepublishing.com
August is National Immunization Awareness Month (NIAM). NIAM raises awareness about why vaccines are important for people of all ages, and how they can prevent serious, deadly, diseases and illnesses.
Immunizations help keep your family and community healthy. Vaccinations are important because they not only protect the person who receives the vaccine, they also help keep diseases from spreading. Immunizations also help protect those who are most vulnerable to these illnesses, such as infants, elders and those with weaker immune systems.
In the U.S., vaccines have reduced infectious diseases that once caused severe illness and death. During NIAM, they encourage you to talk to your doctor, nurse or healthcare professional to ensure that you and your family are protected against serious diseases by getting caught up on routine vaccinations.
As your children head back to school, it's important for your child to be caught up on the recommended vaccines. For more information on the recommended immunization schedules, please visit healthychildren.org/English/safety-prevention/immunizations/Pages/Recommended-Immunization-Scehdules.aspx.
To see if you need any updates on your vaccines, please visit the CDC's adult vaccine assessment tool at www2.cdc.gov/nip/adultimmsched/.

title: City OKs superfund remedial action
description: Rick Patrick rick@greenepublishing.com During the regular meeting of the Madison City Commission on Tuesday, Aug. 13, the commissioners agreed on a plan moving forward with the Consent Decree in U…
content:
Rick Patrick
rick@greenepublishing.com
During the regular meeting of the Madison City Commission on Tuesday, Aug. 13, the commissioners agreed on a plan moving forward with the Consent Decree in United States of America v. City of Madison; ITT LLC (as Successor-in-Interest to ITT Industries, Inc.) and Madison County, Fla. This issue goes back many years and is expected to be going on for many years to come. The issue deals with a mandated clean-up of hazardous materials at the old Rocky Ford landfill, which was once owned by the City of Madison, now owned by Madison County. Years ago, barrels of solvent were placed underground at the site by the old ITT Industries plant. Many of these barrels leaked, causing the material to seep into the water supply. The federal Environmental Protection Agency ordered the material to be cleaned up with ITT sharing a majority of the cost. It was agreed that ITT would pay 60 percent and the City of Madison and Madison County would pay 20 percent each, with a cap of $150,000 in any one year.
Since that time, the hazardous material has been contained to one area and all surrounding residences have been placed on city water, so there is no danger to the public. The material will eventually break down, over the years. In this latest decision, it was decided to allow nature to break the materials down and, if needed, treat any 'hot spots' that may surface. The City Commissioners voted unanimously to accept this plan of action.
The commissioners approved the first reading of an ordinance that would appoint a board to a 'Community Redevelopment Agency' of the City of Madison. This board would consist of citizens from each of the districts who would work to develop a long-term plan for growth of the City of Madison. Each of the current commissioners will recruit citizens from their respective districts to serve on this board.
The commissioners agreed to hire the former inspector for Hamilton County to serve as a part-time building inspector. This agreement passed on a 4-1 vote, with Commissioner Byron Poore casting the dissenting vote.
The commissioners agreed that clean-up after Hurricane Debby should proceed immediately, rather than wait on the Florida Department of Transportation (FDOT). The FDOT has contracted to perform the clean-up, however Commissioner Poore said he 'wanted city roads to be cleaned up now.' It was stated that the City may not receive any reimbursement for the clean-up costs, however that did little to dissuade Commissioner Poore. The commissioners voted unanimously to instruct Madison City Manager Jerome Wyche to have city staff begin cleaning the roadways of debris.
There is a budget workshop meeting planned on Tuesday, Aug. 27, at 5:30 p.m. The meeting will take place in City Hall, located at 321 SW Rutledge St., in Madison.

title: Cowboys take win in Kickoff Classic
description: Rick Patrick rick@greenepublishing.com It was a great opportunity to work out some 'kinks' and get a good look at the 2024 Madison County High School (MCHS) Cowboys varsity football team when they…
content:
Rick Patrick
rick@greenepublishing.com
It was a great opportunity to work out some 'kinks' and get a good look at the 2024 Madison County High School (MCHS) Cowboys varsity football team when they hosted the War Eagles of Wakulla High School on Friday, Aug. 16, in the annual Kickoff Classic football pre-season game. The Cowboys utilized a balanced offense and played a lot of players on their way to a 29-10 win over the War Eagles.
The contest started with the Cowboys on offense. It didn't take long for Cowboy quarterback Ladarius Crumity to connect with Ryshard Miller from 56 yards out for the Cowboys' first score of the evening. After a successful point-after-touchdown (PAT) kick, the Cowboys held a 7-0 lead with 10:25 remaining in the opening quarter. The War Eagles took over at their own 35-yard line. The Cowboys were on the scoreboard again when Sean Williams picked off a pass and returned it to pay-dirt for a Cowboy 'pick-six.' After a successful two-point conversion, the Cowboys had a 15-0 lead, with 8:59 still to play in the first quarter. The rest of the first quarter was typical of teams experiencing their first game play of the season, with turnovers on downs and fumbles. The first quarter ended with the score still 15-0.
Early in the second quarter, the War Eagles managed to drive deep enough into Cowboys territory to boot a field goal, bringing the score to 15-3, with 11:09 still to play in the second quarter. After going three-and-out from their own 25-yard line, the Cowboys had a punt blocked, giving the ball back to the War Eagles at the Cowboys' 33-yard line. The Cowboy defensive unit stiffened and forced another field goal attempt. This time, the kick was off the mark and the Cowboys took over again at their own 20-yard line. That drive went three-and-out and the War Eagles had good field position at the Cowboys' 40-yard-line. The War Eagles took advantage and put together a 60-yard touchdown drive. The score was 15-10, with 4:15 remaining until intermission. The Cowboys went three-and-out from their own 30-yard line. Then, on fourth down, a bad snap on the punt attempt put the War Eagles in control of the pigskin deep in the Cowboys' end of the field. Facing a first and goal at their own five-yard line, the Cowboys avoided disaster when they recovered a fumble at their own 10-yard line. An interception gave the ball back to the War Eagles at the Cowboys' 20-yard line. The Cowboys' defense stiffened again and forced another turnover on downs as the first half drew to a close.
With primarily back-up and junior varsity players seeing action in the second half, it was a good opportunity for both teams to improve the depth of the teams. The War Eagles had the first possession of the second half at their own 29-yard line. That opening drive stalled at the 40-yard line. On the next Cowboy possession, Travis Arnold took the ball and found his way into the secondary before turning on the jets and galloping 52 yards for another Cowboy touchdown. The ensuing two-point conversion attempt failed and the Cowboys held a 21-10 lead, with 6:56 remaining in the third quarter. The Cowboys were able to hold the War Eagles offense to a pair of field goal attempts that both missed their mark. In the waning moments of the contest, a junior varsity Cowboy running back was able to find the end zone, giving the Cowboys their 29-10 lead with less than a minute remaining on the game clock.
The Cowboys racked up a total of 314 yards of offense, with 158 passing yards and 156 yards gained on the ground.
'I was very proud of the effort,' said Head Coach Price Harris. 'There is a lot to fix but I am excited about what this team brings to the table. The physicality and effort was great. We have to clean up some execution and be more disciplined in the little things and cut out some penalties. We have to be better on special teams. All things that can be addressed and fixed.'
The Cowboys will begin their regular season on Friday, Aug. 23, when they travel to DeLand High School to face the Bulldogs. Kickoff is set for 7 p.m. DeLand High School is located at 800 N. Hill Ave., in DeLand, Fla.

title: Checklist for the upcoming fall season
description: Leah Androski reporter@greenepublishing.com With the summer season, coming to an end, here are some things to do around your home to prepare your house for the upcoming fall season. To prepare the …
content:
Leah Androski

With the summer season, coming to an end, here are some things to do around your home to prepare your house for the upcoming fall season.
To prepare the inside of your house for the fall: deep clean your carpets, clean fridge and freezer coils, clean and empty drip trays, replace washers in any interior or exterior faucets, inspect your air and ventilation systems, clean your chimney and fireplace, check/clean exhaust fans in the bathroom, kitchen, laundry room and eliminate any mold and check your washing machine. Also be sure to check your smoke and carbon monoxide detectors, replacing any batteries as needed.
Insects like wasps become more aggressive in late summer. Spray for wasps and eliminate them. Patrolling your property for stagnant water, which can become a breeding ground for mosquitoes. Check the seals around your home, including doors, windows and dryer vents. Inspect the roof for missing/loose/damaged shingles or leaks. Clear any dead twigs and branches in your yard and your gutters. Clean, close and cover your pool.

title: MCSO announces Teen Driver Challenge
description: Leah Androski reporter@greenepublishing.com The Madison County Sheriff's Office (MCSO) recently announced another upcoming date for Teen Driver Challenge. Teen Driver Challenge will be held on Satu…
content:
Leah Androski
reporter@greenepublishing.com
The Madison County Sheriff's Office (MCSO) recently announced another upcoming date for Teen Driver Challenge. Teen Driver Challenge will be held on Saturday, Oct. 26, at the North Florida College (NFC) public safety driving range.
The Teen Driver Challenge classes will be taught by active members of the MCSO who are certified driving instructors and will involve: classroom instruction, driving exercises, test and certificate of completion and traffic stop interaction. Lunch will be provided.
The challenge course skills will include: serpentine, figure eight, evasive driving, vehicle slide recovery, intersection and safe recovery from leaving the road.
Applications are available through school resource deputies, select school officials, at the Madison County Sheriff's Office and by visiting online at www.madisonflsheriff.org.
If you have any questions, please contact Captain Jarrod Lauth at the Madison County Sheriff's Office by calling (850) 253-3322 or emailing him at jarrod.lauth@mcso-fl.org.

title: Legendary Bass Fisherman Hank Parker to speak at Beast Feast in Greenville
description: Bryant Thigpen Contributor Legendary Bass Fisherman Hank Parker will be the guest speaker at the Sixth Annual Beast Feast at St. John's Missionary Baptist Church in Greenville, Florida. The event w…
content:
Bryant Thigpen
Contributor
Legendary Bass Fisherman Hank Parker will be the guest speaker at the Sixth Annual Beast Feast at St. John's Missionary Baptist Church in Greenville, Florida. The event will take place on Saturday, January 18, at 6 p.m. Admission is free. There will be dozens of items, including hunting and fishing gear given away during the event. The Beast Feast will be an evening of fun for the whole family.
According to his biography, Parker has enjoyed a storied professional bass fishing and outdoor television host career that continues to grow each season. His accomplishments on the professional bass fishing tournament trail support the fact he is one of America's greatest bass fishermen to ever compete. Bryant Gumbel, former host of the CBS Morning Show, best described Hank Parker when introducing him as 'the rod-n-reel answer to Michael Jordan, in popularity and talent!"
Parker's professional fishing career started in 1976 when he began fishing the National Bass Association Tournament Circuit, winning their national championship in his first season. For the following two years, he fished both the National Bass Association and American Bass Association. With this success and help from newly acquired sponsors, Hank fished the Bassmaster Tournament Trail.
During his time on the Bassmaster circuit, he won the Bassmaster Classic in 1979 and 1989. Also, he was the first angler to win the B.A.S.S. Grand Slam of Bass Fishing, which includes the Classic, B.A.S.S. Angler of the Year, and the B.A.S.S. SuperBass Tournament. Amazingly, Hank finished "in the money" in 76 percent of the tournaments he fished during his B.A.S.S. career.
In 2003, Hank was inducted into the Bass Fishing Hall of Fame, and in 2006, he was inducted into the Legends of the Outdoors Hall of Fame. Then, in 2014 he was inducted in the International Game Fish Association Hall of Fame. Additionally, Parker is a crowd favorite. He was voted as one of the top 10 greatest anglers of all-time in ESPN's Greatest Angler Debate and listed as one of the 35 most influential people of bass fishing by Bass Anglers Sportsman Society (B.A.S.S.)
Everyone is welcomed to bring a wild-game dish to share and to wear your favorite camo gear. The event will be filled with the best wild game supper, dozens of giveaways and much more!
St. John's Missionary Baptist Church is located at 5905 NW Lovett Road in Greenville, Fla. For more information, please visit www.SJMBCGreenville.com, Facebook.com/SJMBCGreenville, or call (850) 464-0114. We look forward to seeing you there.

title: Brown hired as interim City of Madison manager
description: Mickey Starling: reporter3@greenepublishing.com As the Madison City Commission met on Tuesday, Feb. 11, the city manager's seat was still vacant, with no one in sight to fill the position in the ne…
content:
Mickey Starling: reporter3@greenepublishing.com
As the Madison City Commission met on Tuesday, Feb. 11, the city manager's seat was still vacant, with no one in sight to fill the position in the near future. However, Mayor Judy Townsend and Commissioner Byron Poore proposed offering the job on an interim basis to Madison County Development Council Chair Doug Brown, who expressed willingness to fill in for several months while the commissioners sought another candidate.
After brief discussion, all commissioners agreed that Brown would serve the city well in the position and voted unanimously to offer him the job on a monthly contract until a permanent city manager could be hired. Brown accepted the offer, but jokingly asked that the interim portion of his contract be capitalized. Brown will begin his duties on Monday, Feb. 17.
Shortly after the city manager interviews in January, the Madison City Commission offered the job to Dwayne Flowers, who had held a similar position in Wadley, Ga. After ironing out a contract, Flowers accepted the offer, saying he was '95 percent sure' he would take the job.
After spending a weekend looking for a home to rent and consulting with his family, Flowers' certainty about the position took a turn in the opposite direction, deciding that Madison 'wasn't a good fit' for his family, and he withdrew himself from consideration.

title: Southern Baptists vote on major issues
description: Mickey Starling reporter3@greenepublishing.com The Southern Baptist Convention met in Indianapolis, Ind. on Tuesday, June 11 and Wednesday, June 12 for what is described as the 'world's largest bu…
content:
Mickey Starling
reporter3@greenepublishing.com
The Southern Baptist Convention met in Indianapolis, Ind. on Tuesday, June 11 and Wednesday, June 12 for what is described as the 'world's largest business meeting,' with over 10,000 members present. The convention voted on several issues, but at the forefront were votes concerning in vitro fertilization (IVF) and ordaining women as senior pastors.
The convention opposed the use of IVF, because the process creates a large number of embryos that are never used. A resolution released by the convention called for Baptists 'to reaffirm the unconditional value and right to life of every human being, including those in the embryonic stage, and to only utilize reproductive technologies consistent with that affirmation, especially in the number of embryos generated in the IVF process.' Members were further encouraged to consider adopting embryos that would otherwise be destroyed. The convention overwhelmingly endorsed the belief that embryos are human beings, whether conceived naturally or in a lab.
Last year, the annual meeting saw the removal of two churches over the issue of women serving as senior pastors. That trend continued this year, as First Baptist Church of Alexandria, Virginia was removed from 'friendly cooperation status' due to their status involving women pastors The senior pastor at Alexandria is not a woman, but the church has expressed no opposition to having a woman as the lead pastor. Sixty-one percent of Southern Baptist churches voted the year to exclude women from serving in pastoral leadership. The vote requires 66 percent to pass to become part of their bylaws. The view of some at the convention was that the measure failed because of a 'deeper risk for Baptists.' That risk entails vacating the time-honored tenant of autonomy within the local church. Southern Baptists are not opposed to having women serve as pastors in various ministries within the church, so long as they don't fill the senior pastor's position.

Although aiming to provide footwear to as many people in need as possible, supplies are limited, and the program will prioritize the elderly, physically disabled or ill and those who are economically disadvantaged. title: Lone star tick bites cause severe symptoms
description: Kenzie James news@greenepublishing.com A prevalent tick in northeast Florida has been found to spread numerous illnesses and diseases to humans, causing severe symptoms in patients after tick bites…
content:
Kenzie James
news@greenepublishing.com
A prevalent tick in northeast Florida has been found to spread numerous illnesses and diseases to humans, causing severe symptoms in patients after tick bites.
The Center for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) said the lone star tick is a 'very aggressive tick' that bites humans. Found in the southern and eastern United States, lone star ticks have a light brown back and the females are easily identified by a white spot in the center of their back. The CDC said lone star ticks are known to bite humans in all three stages of life- larvae, nymph and adult. The most common season for tick diseases is spring and summer, when people spend more time outside. June, July and August are the three months when lone star ticks in all three stages are likely to bite humans.
Most ticks can spread lyme disease with their bites, but lone star ticks spread other diseases instead of lyme. These ticks spread rare illnesses, including ehrlichiosis, heartland virus disease, southern tick-associated rash illness (STARI), bourbon virus disease and tularemi. Lone star ticks have also commonly caused alpha-gal syndrome (AGS). Symptoms of these illnesses do not always begin until a few days or weeks after a tick bite. Each disease or illness has specific signs, but common symptoms include:
• Fever
• Chills
• Headaches
• Body aches
• Nausea or vomiting
• Dizziness
AGS, known as 'red meat allergy,' is primarily associated with lone star ticks and causes a patient to have symptoms of an allergic reaction after consuming red meat or red meat products, such as gelatin and milk. In addition to some of the common symptoms listed above, AGS symptoms may include:
• Hives or itchy rash
• Heartburn or indigestion
• Diarrhea
• Cough, shortness of breath or difficulty breathing
• Drop in blood pressure
• Swelling of the lips, throat, tongue or eyelids
• Severe stomach pain
Madison County resident Beth Moore was bitten by a lone star tick about a year ago and was diagnosed with AGS in October of 2023.
'The first reaction I had, I'd eaten a hamburger that evening, and about two in the morning, my hands started itching and my tongue started swelling, I was having trouble breathing,' Moore said. Moore learned in the emergency room that she was in anaphylaxis but did not know what the cause was. A month later, after a similar reaction, Moore did research and a blood test and the doctor diagnosed her with AGS. Moore said she also experienced other AGS symptoms, including stomach cramps and diarrhea, before her first reaction.
Moore said the tick population in Madison has increased significantly in recent years due to the increase in population of white-tailed deer. Deer are one of the main animals lone star ticks feed on, so the increase in deer impacted the population of ticks. The increase in ticks is also reflected in the number of tick bites the Madison County Memorial Hospital (MCMH) has seen. A MCMH data analysis by program manager Kevin Angel showed that there were 34 patients with reported insect or arthropod (tick) bites or stings from quarter four of 2022 through the ongoing quarter two of 2024. Roughly one-third of the total 34 patients were from the current quarter.
'Roughly two months into Quarter Two of 2024, we have seen 12 patients with insect- or arthropod-related bites and stings, nearly double the number seen in Quarter Two of last year,' the data analysis said. The number of patients with insect or tick bites from quarter two of 2023 was seven patients.
Like more common insect bites, there are ways to protect oneself against ticks to try to prevent bites. Dr. Perkins, the Chief Medical Officer at MCMH said the best way to protect against tick bites is tick repellent with DEET, a chemical commonly used in insect and tick repellents.
'Avoid sitting on logs, stumps or the ground. Wear a white long-sleeved shirt so that it is easier to see ticks while they are crawling. Tuck your pants into your socks so they cannot climb up your pants leg,' Perkins said. 'And lastly, periodically inspect your clothes and your body for ticks and remove them before they attach."

title: One small step
description: Hailey Heseltine news@greenepublishing.com July 20, 1969, was a tremendous day in history. This famous day marked vast accomplishments in many fields of science at once, especially astronomy. It al…
content:
Hailey Heseltine
news@greenepublishing.com
July 20, 1969, was a tremendous day in history. This famous day marked vast accomplishments in many fields of science at once, especially astronomy. It also sparked the imagination of millions of people worldwide as an accomplishment that would have seemed impossible only a few decades ago came to life. It was on this day that, with the whole world watching, Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin stepped onto the moon. Tuesday, July 20, 2024, marks the 55th anniversary of this remarkable accomplishment in science.
Apollo 11's landing on the moon was the culmination of countless scientific endeavors over the decades. In fact, flight itself was a relatively new concept. The first plane flew in 1903, yet only 58 years later, mankind had already been to space, and 66 years later, man was on the moon.
Yuri Gagarin, of the Soviet Union, became the first person in space, on April 12, 1961. Only a few years prior, the 'Space Race,' a fierce competition between the United States and the Soviet Union to see who could create the most advanced technology first, had been kicked into action. The competition was based on more than an interest in technology and discovery; it also had strong political implications and could be described as a form of arms race. The tense spirit of competition was one of the things that fueled the two countries to make such large technological leaps in such a short period of time.
A natural subset of the Space Race was the Moon Race. Less than a month after Gagarin's successful orbit and return, John F. Kennedy set a clearly-defined and extremely ambitious goal for America—to have a moon landing before the end of the decade.
That goal guided many of the scientific efforts in the years to follow, when rapid developments in space technology were achieved faster than before. Though some efforts were unsuccessful, with each step, the goal of the moon grew closer. In December of 1968, Apollo 8, a manned spacecraft, successfully orbited the moon ten times and returned back to earth. It was the first time in history humans had left earth's orbit. It was an incredibly risky mission, and yet, it succeeded. Apollo 8 laid the groundwork for the even bigger development to come only a few months later.
On the morning of July 16, 1969, the Apollo 11 launched from Cape Kennedy, Fla., containing three astronauts: Neil Armstrong, Buzz Aldrin and Michael Collins. The mission objective was for the astronauts to land on the moon, experiment, explore, collect samples and extensively document their findings and experience while on the previously uncharted terrain.
Moments from the event were televised through several transmissions, and it was estimated that around 650 million people were watching and waiting from their own homes.
Around 9:30 a.m., Apollo 11 launched, and the world began to hold its breath. A little under three hours later, the spacecraft left Earth's orbit and headed out into the great unknown of space.
The journey to the moon, which is well over 238,000 miles, took the Apollo 11 several days to complete; it began orbiting the moon on July 19, on the afternoon of the third day after launch. Despite the inherent risks of the journey, the flight had remarkably fewer mishaps than were anticipated, and some of the technology designed for emergencies went unused. Multiple transmissions were made from space along the way, featuring Armstrong, Aldrin and Collins, and keeping the viewing world on the edge of its seat.
On July 20, 1969, at 109 hours and 42 minutes, the first human stepped on the moon. Armstrong took that famous 'one small step for man, one giant leap for mankind' before the eyes of millions, followed by Aldrin not long after.
That moment was a cause for worldwide celebration. It marked the success an astounding series of accomplishments in science, proving to the world that it was possible for space travel to progress. Perhaps it seemed that the vast unknown no longer felt quite as unknown, because this instance was proof that it could slowly but surely be explored and studied. The landing was, according to Armstrong, the most worrisome part of the journey, and if it was accomplished, then surely other developments could be as well.
Armstrong and Aldrin placed an American flag on the surface of the moon, explored, collected samples, took photographs and left commemorative memorabilia, including some in honor of fallen astronauts, such as the Apollo 1 crew.
The journey back home was also a success; the astronauts landed in the Pacific Ocean near Hawaii and were recovered by the U.S.S. Hornet on July 24. On that day, Armstrong, Aldrin and Collins brought more than just samples home with them—they brought inspiration and hope to the world. They proved that it was possible for humans to travel farther than previously thought. They had stepped onto another celestial body, and survived to tell the tale. This was not just a one-time instance, either—it was proof that it could be done again.
That one small step, which was the product of the diligent research and planning of thousands, truly made history.

title: City sets tentative millage rate
description: Rick Patrick rick@greenepublishing.com During the regular meeting of the Madison City Commission on Tuesday, July 9, the commissioners agreed on a tentative millage rate for the city. The proposed…
content:
Rick Patrick
rick@greenepublishing.com
During the regular meeting of the Madison City Commission on Tuesday, July 9, the commissioners agreed on a tentative millage rate for the city. The proposed millage rate would remain at seven mills. This means property owners would pay seven dollars in property tax per $1,000 of property value. If a piece of property was valued at $100,000, the property owner would pay $700 in property tax. The total tax levied at the proposed millage rate would be $839,855. The first public hearing for the fiscal year 2024/2025 budget is set for Monday, Sept. 9, at 5:30 p.m., in City Hall, located at 321 SW Rutledge St., in Madison.
The commissioners approved a plan to invest excess funds the city has. This will allow the city to receive a better return on excess funds. Such investments are authorized under Florida law and the investments will be safe and the money will be available, if needed for emergencies.
There was discussion regarding using $30,000 of excess funds received from the county through the Small County Surtax. It was proposed to use the money for the purchase of a third police vehicle.
The commissioners approved lease agreement with RDK Assets, Inc. for a 2024 Freightliner Rear Loader and two 2024 Freightliner grapples. The lease terms would be for 13 months, with a rate of $6,250 per month for the rear loader and $6,500 per month for each of the grapples.
There was discussion regarding a recreational vehicle and shed that has been placed on vacant residential property on SE Stephens Avenue. The discussion centered around the question of whether the owner of the recreational vehicle is in violation of land-use codes by placing the recreational vehicle and shed on the property. The owner suggested he was being singled out. Commissioner Byron Poore provided photographs of other possible violations and questioned why those instances were not being enforced. Mayor Judy Townsend stated if those other examples were in violation, codes should be enforced in those cases as well. Mayor Townsend said enforcement should be uniform. At that point, Commissioner Poore left the meeting, voicing an apology to the recreational vehicle owner.
The next item on the agenda was a street paving plan, placed on the agenda by Commissioner Poore. The item was tabled in light of Commissioner Poore's absence.
The next scheduled meeting of the Madison City Commission is scheduled to take place on Tuesday, Aug. 13, at 5:30 p.m. The meeting will take place in City Hall, located at 321 SW Rutledge St., in Madison.

title: Former Cowboy on pre-season award list
description: Rick Patrick rick@greenepublishing.com Madison County High School (MCHS) graduate and former Cowboy football star Zane Herring was recently named to the watchlist for the prestigious Outland Troph…
content:
Rick Patrick
rick@greenepublishing.com
Madison County High School (MCHS) graduate and former Cowboy football star Zane Herring was recently named to the watchlist for the prestigious Outland Trophy for the 2024 college football season. Herring began his college football career at Florida State University (FSU), before transferring to the University of South Florida (USF), in Tampa, Fla. He is one of 75 interior linemen, both offense and defense, from across the nation, chosen by the Football Writers Association of America (FWAA).
The FWAA will announce the Outland Trophy semifinalists on Wednesday, Nov. 20, with the three finalists named on Tuesday, Nov. 26. The winner of the Outland Trophy will be announced during the 'Home Depot College Football Awards,' live on ESPN on Thursday, Dec. 12.
In addition to being named to the Outland Trophy watchlist, Herring has been named First Team Preseason All-Conference (American Athletic Conference) by both Lindy's and Athlon. Phil Steele selected Herring to the second team All-AAC.
Herring graduated from FSU with a Bachelor of Science degree in Marketing. He is currently taking more business classes at USF in order to earn a second bachelor's degree.
The USF Bulls open their season on Saturday, Aug. 31 against Bethune-Cookman University, in Raymond James Stadium, in Tampa.
Zane is the son of Sean and April Herring.

title: Four vehicle crash results in fatality
description: Rick Patrick rick@greenepublishing.com According to a report from the Florida Highway Patrol (FHP), a crash on Interstate 10 (I-10) claimed the life of a 39-year-old Ocoee, Fla. man. The crash occ…
content:
Rick Patrick
rick@greenepublishing.com
According to a report from the Florida Highway Patrol (FHP), a crash on Interstate 10 (I-10) claimed the life of a 39-year-old Ocoee, Fla. man. The crash occurred at approximately 7:15 p.m. on Wednesday, Aug. 7, on I-10 near mile marker 266.
The report states that a van, driven by the 39-year-old Ocoee, Fla. man was traveling west on I-10, in the inside lane. A pick-up truck, driven by a 24-year-old man from Mount Dora, Fla., was also traveling west on I-10, in the outside lane. A sport utility vehicle, driven by a 61-year-old Chipley, Fla. man was traveling east on I-10. Another vehicle, a tractor/trailer was also traveling east, directly behind the sport utility vehicle. The van left the roadway and entered the grassy median. The driver of the van attempted to regain control of the vehicle and re-entered the roadway. After re-entering the roadway, the van's right side struck the pick-up truck's left side. The driver of the van lost control, crossing the grassy median and entering the eastbound lanes, while traveling west. The van collided with the SUV, causing the SUV to leave the roadway to the right and rollover. The tractor/trailer then collided with the van head-on. The van came to a final rest in the median, facing south. The pick-up truck came to a final rest in the north shoulder of I-10, facing west. The SUV came to a final rest in the south grassy shoulder/ditch, facing south. The tractor/trailer came to a final rest on the south shoulder of I-10, facing northeast.
The driver of the van suffered fatal injuries in the crash. The other three drivers involved received minor injuries. A passenger in the pick-up truck was not injured.
The FHP was assisted at the scene and during the investigation by Madison County Fire Rescue and the Madison County Sheriff's Office.
