title: Marie Smith – Candidate for Property Appraiser
description: HI, I am Marie Risoli Smith, candidate for Property Appraiser. I am a lifelong resident of Madison County, and the 4th generation to live and work on our family ranch, raising commercial beef cattl…
content:
HI, I am Marie Risoli Smith, candidate for Property Appraiser. I am a lifelong resident of Madison County, and the 4th generation to live and work on our family ranch, raising commercial beef cattle. I have been happily married for 21 years to Travis Smith and together we have one son, Blaine who is 18. I am an active member of the Big Bend Cattlewomen's Association; I have always enjoyed volunteering my time with youth organizations such as Babe Ruth baseball/softball and junior rodeo. I began my career with the Madison County Property Appraisers office in November of 2001 as a field appraiser and I am currently the direct assistant to the Property Appraiser. I appreciate the opportunity provided by Greene Publishing to speak to you all today. My goal is to prove to you that my years of experience and vast knowledge of this office make me the most qualified candidate to protect the interest of the property owners of Madison County.
Question 1 Answer:
I bring 23 years of experience to this office. I work with the citizens of Madison every day, filing for exemptions or answering questions they may have on deeds or parcel information. We are a small office, so over the years, I have acquired many different skills such as field appraisal, deed specialist, budget administrator, accounts payable, value adjustment board presentations, and website administrator, I work directly with the Department of Revenue with sales qualification studies, tax roll edits, and most recently training for tax roll certification. I know what it takes to run this office effectively and efficiently while prioritizing taxpayers' interests. To be an effective leader, you must first know the job. I know this job! I have been blessed to work with a wonderful staff, and once elected together, we will continue to be one of the most respected Property Appraiser offices in the state.
Question 2 Answer:
One of the biggest challenges in our community is Growth; with growth comes change, and that can be difficult for a small community. With this growth, we have seen a significant increase in market value, which has resulted in an increase in property value. For those of us with a homestead exemption, that increase is minimal, up to 3%. Still, for those with multiple properties, inherited property, or just moving into our community the increase in values can be a heavy burden. As your Property Appraiser, I will remain diligent in keeping the community aware of the benefits they are entitled to and remain active with the Property Appraisers Association of Florida to be an advocate for the local taxpayers as a voice for legislation that best suits our community.
Question 3 Answer:
The primary role of the Property Appraiser office is to place value and grant exemptions on all real estate and tangible personal property. Values are based on the previous year's sales of like properties. This office is governed by the Florida Statutes and the Department of Revenue. The tax roll is audited yearly by the Department of Revenue to ensure all properties are being assessed fairly so that no property is over or underassessed according to the current market value. The Property Appraisers office also maintains aerial maps with current deed changes and issues GIS/911 addressing which is instrumental in law enforcement and ambulance services. The values obtained by this office are used to generate the county's ad valorum tax base. The real estate market determines property value, and this office is responsible for reflecting that. The property Appraiser does not set your taxes; nor is the office a taxing authority, this office does not set millage rates, mail out tax bills, nor collect taxes. When a property changes names, exemptions and classifications must be renewed, I have been instrumental in carrying out new policies that go above and beyond to make the new owners aware of the benefits available through this office: such as traditional mail, emails, phone calls, and even social media communications. As Property Appraiser my team and I will continue to advance with the latest technology, as well as maintain the open-door policies and friendly customer service you have grown accustomed to.
My 23 years in this field and in this office have prepared me to be the next Property Appraiser of Madison County. I have devoted my career to serving the property owners of this County. When elected I will ensure my team and I operate an office that the property owners of Madison can trust has their best interest at heart. I have learned over the years this position requires dedication, professionalism as well as compassion, all qualities that I possess, but the most important quality a person can have is being honest. The challenge of the Property Appraiser is honesty is not always the preferred answer, but rest assured it is always THE answer. I will operate this office openly and honestly putting the taxpayer's best interest first.
I would love to talk with you if you have questions or comments about me or this office. Feel free to reach out by phone 850-464-8205 or Facebook Marie R Smith for Property Appraiser. I appreciate all the support I have been receiving and I ask that you please get out and vote Smith for Property Appraiser! Early voting starts August 10th

title: Jonathan Mazzella – Candidate for Superintendent of Schools
description: My name is Jonathan Mazzella and I am running for Superintendent of Schools as a Republican. My beautiful wife, Karon Mazzella, and I have two children that go to public school right here in Madiso…
content:
My name is Jonathan Mazzella and I am running for Superintendent of Schools as a Republican. My beautiful wife, Karon Mazzella, and I have two children that go to public school right here in Madison County, one at Lee Elementary and one at Madison County High School.
After speaking with hundreds of community members, a common theme emerged: the need for a Superintendent with a strong business mindset. The role of Superintendent is essentially the CEO of the public school system. My wife, Karon Mazzella, and I own businesses here in Madison, Florida, where we have employed dozens of local residents over the years. With 16 years of leadership experience in the Marine Corps and Army, I have honed my ability to work effectively with people from diverse backgrounds. I've learned how to leverage a person's individual skill sets and cultivate new ones to achieve our shared goals, which in this case, is providing exceptional service to our customers. In addition to my military experience, I have over five years of business experience, serving thousands of local residents and visitors. I've developed a deep understanding of customer care and actively teach my employees to provide genuine service with both love, respect and duty. I believe these skills and experiences fulfill the needs of the community for a business mindset, and make me a viable option for the position of Superintendent of Schools.
Question 1:
Having been a ServSafe manager and restaurant owner for many years, I'm well-versed in maintaining food safety. Our approach involves multiple layers of protection against foodborne illness. It all begins with establishing strong relationships with high-quality food distributors. Upon delivery, we thoroughly inspect all food items to ensure they are properly labeled, dated, and that the containers are in good condition. If any issues are found, we refuse the shipment and alert our food distributor so corrections can be made quickly. Food storage is another critical area. We ensure that all items are kept at the correct temperatures—whether frozen, refrigerated, or in dry storage. Regular monitoring of temperatures and inventory is essential. We also follow FIFO (First In, First Out) to use older stock before newer items. Despite these precautions, it's still possible for spoiled food to go unnoticed until it is cooked. Therefore, it's crucial that the serving line staff can quickly and accurately assess and discard any suspect food without contaminating the rest. Effective management of food safety comes down to thorough employee training and consistent procedural follow-ups. I am confident in my ability to uphold these standards and retrain staff as needed.
Food is a passion of mine, and I'm committed to enhancing both the taste and nutrition of school meals while adhering to federal guidelines. I plan to work closely with the food service supervisor and the food service warehouse manager to develop more flavorful and nutritious meals that comply with the National School Lunch Program (NSLP) and the School Breakfast Program (SBP) regulations. These programs have strict requirements regarding calorie content, saturated fat, salt, sugar, and whole grain usage. While I'd love to replicate the taste of our Cucinella's spaghetti in school meals, I understand that we must operate within these nutritional guidelines. My goal is to make school lunches both enjoyable and healthy, balancing flavor with compliance to create meals that are both appealing and aligned with regulatory standards. I look forward to the challenge of improving the taste of school meals while staying within these important nutritional rules.
Question 2:
A fair, firm, and consistent approach is essential for effective disciplinary action in schools. However, achieving this requires support from teachers, parents, and students, as enforcing discipline can be challenging. Bullying, harassment, and threats must be addressed from the home, where it's crucial for parents to reinforce that such behavior will not be tolerated. When these values are instilled at home, students are more likely to understand that their actions are unacceptable at school. Children often don't fully grasp the impact of their actions on others. Thus, when disciplinary issues arise, it's important to address them promptly and fairly, adhering to established guidelines. Consistency is key; if a principal or teacher makes a disciplinary decision, it should be upheld, even if a parent tries to downplay or dispute it. Students should come to school ready to learn and leave any personal issues at home. When faculty members encounter inappropriate behavior, such as cursing in the hallways, it's crucial to apply consistent disciplinary measures to all involved. Ignoring or dismissing these behaviors only allows problems to escalate. I've seen firsthand how a single negative influence can impact an entire environment (where one bad apple spoils the bunch). When every student and family understands the expected behavior, it helps establish a self-correcting culture. This awareness creates an environment where issues are addressed promptly, and positive behavior is reinforced, benefiting the entire community.
Creating a culture where discipline is respected requires the entire community's involvement, starting with home education and then reinforced at school. By fostering a culture that clearly communicates and upholds standards of behavior, we ensure that both students and staff understand the importance of discipline and its role in a productive learning environment.
Question 3:
Five years from now I envision a community where every parent is actively involved in their child's education. Where Madison County has fostered a culture that teaches from home that bullying, harassment, and inappropriate language are unacceptable. A community that each and every child knows they are expected to maintain a certain level of respect, dignity, and teachable demeanor so that our staff can do their jobs in helping them excel at life.
I want to get there by enhancing the public school district's image, transforming it into an institution renowned for academic excellence and professionalism. In this vision, our schools would be recognized for having exceptional teachers who are well-compensated and proud of their work. Parents and students alike would understand that they are part of a culture that upholds high standards of behavior and professionalism, where right and wrong are clearly defined. I want students to set and achieve personal goals, and understand that their great efforts in high school will ease their transition into adulthood. Above all, I aim for our community to take pride in being part of Madison, offering mutual support, advice, love and kindness, rather than criticism and judgment.I want my service to benefit everyone in our community—from our youngest kindergarten students to our teachers, parents, leaders, workforce and retiree's—to not only survive but also thrive in this great big world.

content:
It has been my pleasure visiting with the residents in District 2, during the past 5 months. If we haven't been able to connect in person, please do not hesitate to contact me.
You are important to me!
* Married to Dale Gibson; one son Bill Gibson; daughter in law Kelsey; granddaughter Harper; grandson Carter.

* Retired after many years in the public school system allowing; the time to represent/attend the many wonderful events in our schools; time to prepare for meetings/workshops, as well as being accessible to the public at all times.
* Elected to the school board in August 2016, after attending school board meetings for five years, as an interested educator/tax payer.
* Consistent and dedicated involvement in our schools by; teaching monthly enrichment lessons in ALL five elementary schools, which provides the students and myself with both knowledge and enjoyment; sponsoring/contributing to the many school events; as well as providing academic incentives. I do this as I am able, and feel that it helps the schools/students thrive.
* My husband and I have always and will continue to support the local fire departments, law enforcement, churches, and of course our schools.
Questions 1 Answer:
1. How will the school system insure that our children are getting safe, healthy and nutritious food at school?
All food service complaints are brought to the attention and addressed immediately. The school food service department follows strict guidelines. Specific meal patterns are designed for the various grade levels, (k-5, 6-8, 9-12). The Department of Health regulates food service establishments such as schools.
Inspections take place 4 times a year.
I personally have visited/eaten in all of the lunchrooms many times. I see immaculate kitchens, friendly loving workers, and delicious food being served. For some children it's the only meal they'll receive that day.
A big thanks to Mrs Iris Wynn and her staff!
Questions 2 Answer:
All bullying/harassment/threats are addressed immediately and taken seriously. Each offense has specific consequences, all very plainly laid out in the student handbook that each student receives at the beginning of the school year.
This brochure goes home with each student.
Parents have the opportunity to review the offenses, sign and return the enclosed form to the students teacher. Parents are encouraged to report any offenses as soon as they occur.
The school system strives to provide a safe and secure learning experience for all students.
Questions 3 Answer:
We have wonderful things going on in all of our schools. I know this as I am deeply involved in the goings on at our schools. Lots of hard work and dedication goes on each and every day.
Due to a decision made by three board members in July to close the community schools, the future of Madison County School System is unclear at this point. Parents choose where their children will be educated. They know their child better than anyone else.
A year from now, approximately 400 students will be displaced. Many parents and teachers have already made their decision about the future. We have lost many excellent teachers due to the uncertainty of the schools.
As a board member I will continue to support our schools. Always with an eye on the bottom line, making sure our teachers, students and employees have what they need to be successful!
It has been and honor and a privilege to represent district #2 on the Madison School Board. I want to thank you for placing your trust in me eight years ago. I have and will continue to focus on providing a quality education for all students.
Thank you for your support!
Carol Gibson

title: Avoid being scammed with post-Debby insurance claims
description: Danny Federico news@greenepublishing.com In the aftermath of Hurricane Debby, many Floridians are expected to file insurance claims for wind and flood damage. The Florida Association of Public Insu…
content:
Danny Federico
news@greenepublishing.com
In the aftermath of Hurricane Debby, many Floridians are expected to file insurance claims for wind and flood damage. The Florida Association of Public Insurance Adjusters (FAPIA) emphasizes the importance of timely documentation and filing of insurance claims to ensure that affected individuals receive the necessary support.
However, homeowners are also warned to be cautious of potential scams during this vulnerable time. The association highlights that homeowners should be wary of anyone offering a "free roof" or financial incentives to file claims on their behalf. Additionally, offers of payment for home inspections should raise red flags. FAPIA provides seven essential tips to help Floridians avoid becoming victims of insurance fraud:
Verify Professional Licensing: Ensure that contractors and public insurance adjusters are licensed to operate in Florida. Only public adjusters and lawyers are legally authorized to negotiate claims with insurance companies. Verification can be done at www.beclaimsmart.com.
Check for Required Permits: Confirm that all necessary permits for repairs are obtained. Failure to do so may result in incomplete or substandard work and potential liability for the homeowner.
Avoid Cash Payments: Use traceable payment methods such as credit cards, checks or debit cards. Always request and keep receipts for insurance claims.
Beware of "Assignment of Benefits" (AOB) Agreements: Recent legislation has made it illegal to ask customers to sign AOB agreements, which allow third parties to manage insurance claims and collect payouts. Individuals who find such requests are urged to report them to the Department of Financial Services.
Timely Filing of Claims: Florida law mandates that hurricane damage claims be filed within one year of the loss. Prompt inspection and claim filing are crucial.
Mitigate Further Damage: To avoid claim denial, take steps to prevent additional damage to property, such as tarping a damaged roof. Review your insurance policy's "Duties After Loss" section for specific responsibilities.
Stay Alert for Scammers: Be cautious of individuals posing as contractors or roofers offering to handle insurance claims. Only licensed public insurance adjusters and attorneys should manage these claims.
Public insurance adjusters are trained to conduct thorough property inspections, document damages, understand policies, inform policyholders of their responsibilities, estimate repair costs accurately, and ethically navigate the claims process.
For more information and to find a licensed public adjuster, visit www.beclaimsmart.com.

title: 4-H travels to Cloudland Canyon State Park
description: Lauren Williams, 4-H Club Leader Contributor On Saturday, July 20, Madison County 4-H'ers with the Saddles and Spurs 4-H Club traveled to Cloudland Canyon State Park in Rising Fawn, Ga. for four d…
content:
Lauren Williams, 4-H Club Leader
Contributor
On Saturday, July 20, Madison County 4-H'ers with the Saddles and Spurs 4-H Club traveled to Cloudland Canyon State Park in Rising Fawn, Ga. for four days.
These hardworking kids and their families raise money for an annual trip selling concessions at the North Florida Livestock Show and Sale. These monies also fund educational activities throughout the year. Each family visited Cherokee Falls, Hemlock Falls and the Overlook Trail at Cloudland Canyon witnessing incredible views and wildlife. Eighteen individuals stayed in a group lodge and enjoyed delicious meals prepared by club members.
On Monday, July 22, the families traveled to Chattanooga, Tenn. to visit the Tennessee Aquarium, the Calvin Coolidge Medal of Honor Museum and the Tennessee Valley Railroad. They got a self-guided tour of the Aquarium and learned about our nation's finest heroes at the Medal of Honor Museum. They also boarded the Missionary Ridge Local Train Ride for an hour-long tour crossing four bridges and a Pre-Civil War tunnel. This was the first time many of the members had ever ridden on a train. The kids also completed the Cloudland Canyon State Park Junior Ranger program, earning pins and badges.
The program consists of learning about the unique features of the park and being respectful of our natural resources. The trip was a great learning experience and enjoyed by all. For more information or to join 4-H, families interested can contact 4-H Extension Agent, Beth Moore, at (850) 973-4138 at the Madison County Extension Office, located at 184 College Loop, in Madison.

title: National Security: Chameleon
description: A chameleon is a class of rain forest lizards that has the unique capability to change colors depending on their surroundings. It is a form of camouflage and defensive mechanism for the reptile. Th…
content:
A chameleon is a class of rain forest lizards that has the unique capability to change colors depending on their surroundings. It is a form of camouflage and defensive mechanism for the reptile. They can defeat predators by blending in with their surroundings and becoming invisible.
Sometimes, we identify politicians as 'chameleons' where they 'change their stripes' as a form of political expedient. It is a way to hide their true identity or belief system. This is a criticism of Vice President Kamala Harris. In more than a month since becoming the Democratic nominee for president under very unusual circumstances, she has not given a single interview nor answered questions from the press. She has given speeches from teleprompters at big rallies, but that isn't the same as answering tough questions, especially about inconsistencies of policies she has previously advocated and now changed … maybe. Some have given her the nickname 'Hiding Harris.'
In the past, she has publicly advocated for many extremely liberal or even socialist policies. Anonymous members of her campaign say she has changed from the stances she took as a new US Senator (2017-21) and during her unsuccessful presidential campaign for the Democratic nomination (2019-20). But she hasn't explained the changes herself or why her positions have changed on things like fracking, Medicare for all, defunding police, etc. Is she changing to get elected, only to backtrack when taking office?
In March 2021, just two months after becoming vice president, she was appointed by President Biden to address the root causes of illegal migration that was then just beginning to overwhelm our southern border. Specifically, she was tasked to address issues in the Northern Triangle of Central America and Mexico. She made one foray down to the region and gave away a pot of money. She never visited the border itself to understand the magnitude of the problem or speak with those most affected.
Whether or not she was the 'border czar' as some claim or not, she failed spectacularly. Illegal immigration under the Biden-Harris Administration is more than 250 percent higher than during the same time period of the Trump Administration. It appears that more than 15 million illegal immigrants have entered this country since the beginning of the Biden-Harris Administration. This is not an accident; it is by design.
This mass of humanity now sprinkled throughout the country has brought with it a host of problems, including crime, illicit drugs like fentanyl and human trafficking. Not all these immigrants are bad, but they are unvetted and, good or bad, bring many problems associated with language differences and services. Imagine the effect on schools.
When she was running for president four years ago, she said that she would close all migrant detention centers on day one. So, what is her policy now? How would she fix this mess? No answer. She said back then that ICE (Immigration and Customs Enforcement) would need to be reimagined and begin anew. What is her plan? What would be the mission of a reimagined ICE? No answer.
In the summer of 2020, following George Floyd's death, as Minneapolis ($500 million worth of damage) and other cities burned, she asked her supporters to contribute the Minnesota Freedom Fund to bail out the arsonists. What is her position on the violent crime that plagues our cities? These two issues, illegal immigration and crime, juxtapose. Think of how many victims of these horror stories are young women like Laken Riley, Rachel Moran and Jocelyn Nungaray. Is this Kamela's accidental war on women?
Now, she says that she favors price controls on groceries. That is a hare brain-scheme if I've ever heard of one. Her economic plan does not have a single element associated with growing the economy. I don't think she understands how to do such a thing. All her economic policies call for government spending which created the inflation we're now experiencing. Since Kamala became vice president, the price of groceries has risen 20 percent and that is not coming down. Too many dollars chasing too few goods.
So, if you look at Kamala's answers to the big three – economy, border and crime – her responses (or lack thereof) are all bad. And just to underscore the point, when you go to the Harris-Walz website, there are no policy positions listed, only buttons to click for donations. What are her policies? Only Silence.
About 40 years ago, a soft rock group named Culture Club, led by Boy George, recorded a number one hit, Karma Chameleon. The song is about someone living a lie. Here is a chorus line that is telling: 'I'm a man without conviction; I'm a man who doesn't know; How to sell a contradiction; You come and go; you come and go.' Where does Kamala Chameleon stand? Inquiring minds what to know.

content:

The 55-Plus Club kicked off a new season of monthly luncheon meetings on Wednesday, Sept. 11, with a program provided by Madison County Sheriff David Harper and members of the K-9 team from the Madison County Sheriff's Office (MCSO). The program also included demonstrations of the skills of the dogs and their handlers.
The 55 Plus Club meets on the second Wednesday of each month, from September through April, at the United Methodist Center, located approximately five miles north of Madison, on Highway 145 (Colin Kelly Hwy.). The luncheon meetings are free of charge and open to any Madison County resident, 55 years of age or older. The luncheon begins at noon, followed by a different program each month.
For more information about the 55 Plus Club, or any other outreach ministry of the United Methodist Cooperative Ministries, please contact Deborah Brown at (850) 253-2133.

title: Madison County Sheriff's Office announces 'Operation Get Home Safe'
description: Rick Patrick rick@greenepublishing.com In an effort to keep impaired drivers off the road and to provide a safer New Year's holiday, the Madison County Sheriff's Office (MCSO) has announced they w…
content:
Rick Patrick
rick@greenepublishing.com
In an effort to keep impaired drivers off the road and to provide a safer New Year's holiday, the Madison County Sheriff's Office (MCSO) has announced they will again be offering a safe and free local ride home to anyone who may be impaired on Tuesday, Dec. 31. The service will be available from 10 p.m. on Tuesday, Dec. 31, until 6 a.m. on Wednesday, Jan. 1. The number to call is (850) 973-4001. People are asked to please not call 911 for a ride home.
According to the MCSO, 'recent data shows December drunk driving deaths are the highest in almost 15 years. As a result, the MCSO is partnering with the National Highway Transportation and Safety Administration (NHTSA) and the Florida Department of Transportation (FDOT) to support 'Drive Sober or Get Pulled Over.' As part of this campaign, which runs through the New Year holiday, it is likely that motorists will see a greater number of law enforcement officials on the roads throughout the holiday season. The MCSO reminds everyone:
• Never drink and drive
• Don't allow someone to get behind the wheel if that person has been drinking
• If you are hosting a gathering, make sure everyone has a sober ride home
• Call 911 if you see a drunk driver
• Always wear your seat belt; this is your best defense against impaired drivers.
Greene Publishing, Inc. wishes everyone a safe and prosperous New Year.

title: The Florida Future Chef competition is accepting student applications
description: Kenzie James news@greenepublishing.com The annual Florida Future Chef competition, sponsored by the Florida Department of Agriculture and Consumer Services, is currently accepting applications for …
content:
Kenzie James
news@greenepublishing.com
The annual Florida Future Chef competition, sponsored by the Florida Department of Agriculture and Consumer Services, is currently accepting applications for contestants for the 2024 competition.
Students from seven-years-old to 13-years-old are invited to enter the competition, with a short video of themselves preparing their favorite dish using in-season Florida ingredients. The prompt for the competition is to 'recreate or elevate a school meal,' according to the Florida Future Chef website. Students are asked to make one of their favorite lunch meals unique by adding their own take, such as different spices, more produce or taking inspiration from a family recipe. Additionally, chefs must use at least one Fresh from Florida ingredient. The list of in-season ingredients can be found at https://followfreshfromflordia.com/.
To enter, a student's cooking video must be between two and five minutes long and show them preparing the dish. The judging panel will evaluate the videos 50 percent on appearance and 50 percent on presentation and creativity. Three finalists will be selected and notified around Monday, July 22 and will be invited to an in-person finale in September. The winner of the competition will earn $5,000; second place will receive $3,000; and third place will receive $2,000, all through Florida Prepaid. The Florida Future Chef competition can be a way to start a young chef's career. Last year's champion, Remy, recently competed on MasterChef Junior season nine and was one of the runners-up.
The entry period for the 2024 competition is open for students to submit videos until Friday, July 12. Entry forms and additional information can be found at https://floridafuturechef.com.

title: Madison Public Library holds drum circle
description: Leah Androski reporter@greenepublishing.com The Madison Public Library, located at 378 College Loop, in Madison, held a drum circle, celebrating the kick-off for their summer programs. On Thursday,…
content:
Leah Androski
reporter@greenepublishing.com
The Madison Public Library, located at 378 College Loop, in Madison, held a drum circle, celebrating the kick-off for their summer programs.
On Thursday, June 13, the Madison Public Library held the drum circle for the public to come and participate in. Clinton and Violet Tipton brought their African drums and encouraged the public to come jam out with them.
The Tipton's started the drum circle by telling people to pick a drum, sit by it and start playing. They gave tips on how to best position the drum in order to play effectively. They also showed how the drums could be tuned, giving them a better sound.
Clinton began to explain a game to the other drummers, where he would raise his hands and lower his hands. The raising and lowering of the hands would determine the volume at which the drums were played. The lower his hands the quieter the drums would be played. After playing this game for a while, Clinton decided to bring out other instruments rather than just the drums. After this Clinton brought out a cowbell.
Clinton called this next activity 'Bell Power.' He would play the cow bell and ask everyone who was playing the drums to play back the same thing on their drums. After playing 'bell power,' he then sat back down and encouraged anyone who wanted to dance to do so.
After the dance party, the Tipton's told a story about the different ways to play a drum. The story started off with a lonely little ant, which Clinton played the drum with one hand. When the ant finds a friend, Clinton then added another hand while playing the drum. After introducing a couple other animals each causing everyone to bang the drum a different way, the Tiptons told the participants to play their favorite animal.

title: Forgotten Coast K9: How you can help change lives
description: Heather Ainsley news@greenepublishing.com For men and women who have put their lives on the line to serve our nation, adjusting to civilian life can be a huge mental, emotional and even physical c…
content:
Heather Ainsley
news@greenepublishing.com
For men and women who have put their lives on the line to serve our nation, adjusting to civilian life can be a huge mental, emotional and even physical challenge. Many veterans and first responders have seen and lived through horrors the rest of us can hardly imagine, leaving them with crippling anxiety, depression and PTSD. For many service members, retired or still in duty, a service dog can be the key to living a normal life, as these dogs provide security, emotional and medical support.
These dogs don't come cheap, though, and many service personnel who desperately need a service dog cannot afford one, and those who find charity programsusually end up on a waiting list for years to come.
Forgotten Coast K9 is a veteran owned and operated non-profit 501(c)(3) organization, and strives to provide certified service dogs to veterans and first responders at minimal to no cost. A single canine that has completed the necessary certification can cost anywhere from $25,000 to $40,000, a price most veterans are unable to afford. Forgotten Coast K9's partnerships allow them to limit out of pocket expense to just $5,000. Forgotten Coast K9 also raises money for service members who are unable to afford a canine to participate in their programs at little to no cost. They rely solely on donations from the public and fundraising efforts to make this possible.
Forgotten Coast K9 is operated by Chris O'Brian, who initially created the company as a canine training company, focusing not just on training dogs, but on instructing owners how to train and work with their own dogs. While the company was seeing success in their endeavors, he began to see the need for a different direction the company could go. In 2021, he turned his training company into a non-profit organization dedicated to pairing veterans in need with life-changing service dogs.
Because not every veteran or first responder may need a full-blown service dog, Forgotten Coast K9 also offers Emotional Support dogs. Their Emotional Support Dogs for Veterans program provides an emotional support dog to veterans and first responders who need a trained companion to help them through their daily life. These dogs are are trained in high level obedience, have a solid baseline for advanced training, and are conditioned to handle emotional or intense situations better than an everyday pet.
Forgotten Coast K9 also provides fundraising efforts for veterans who are unable to afford a dog, and are committed to getting dogs paired with the handlers who need them. There are several ways to donate:
Donations are tax deductible, and can be sent to Forgotten Coast K9 directly, at 137 SW Shelby Ave. in Madison, Fla., 32340. The organization also accepts donations through CashApp and Venmo and can be found under the name $forgottencoastk9 (CashApp) and @forgottencoastk9 (Venmo). They also accept donations through their website, Forgottencoastk9.org and on their Facebook page.
Anyone wishing to apply for a Forgotten Coast K9 service or emotional support dog, or for more information on how you can help, you can reach O'Brian online at ForgottencoastK9.org.

title: The Bush Wealth Advantage: Protect against a scorching market and weather – Intense summer heat and hot stock market both demand a careful approach
description: As the first days of summer arrive, the nation finds itself in the grip of two concurrent heat waves: one from the atmosphere, and one from the financial markets. While an intense heat dome blanket…
content:
As the first days of summer arrive, the nation finds itself in the grip of two concurrent heat waves: one from the atmosphere, and one from the financial markets. While an intense heat dome blankets the Midwest and Northeast, driving temperatures to record-breaking highs, the stock market, led by the S&P 500 and NASDAQ, is also experiencing unprecedented surges.
The current heat wave and the buoyant stock market share more than just a metaphorical similarity; both phenomena demand a proactive approach to ensure well-being and financial stability.
The Heat Wave: A Meteorological Menace
This year's most significant heat event is upon us, as an expansive heat dome fuels a prolonged and intense heat wave. The Midwest and Northeast are set to experience record-breaking high temperatures well into the coming week. This climatic phenomenon is characterized by stagnant high-pressure systems trapping heat in the lower atmosphere, leading to sweltering conditions. With temperatures soaring above normal and little respite in sight, the heat wave poses substantial risks to health, infrastructure, and daily life.
The Market Surge: A Financial Heat Wave
Simultaneously, the stock market is experiencing its own form of a heat wave. The S&P 500 and NASDAQ have recently hit record highs, reflecting robust investor confidence and economic optimism.
This rally is driven by a combination of factors, including strong corporate earnings, easing inflation concerns, and continued innovation in technology sectors. However, just like the weather, financial markets can be unpredictable and subject to rapid changes.
Protect Your Wealth from the Financial Heat
As investors bask in the warmth of a booming market, it's crucial to take steps to ensure that portfolios do not wilt under the pressure of scorching records. Here are some strategies to help protect your investments during these high-temperature times:
Diversification: Just as you would seek shade to escape the heat, diversifying your portfolio can protect you from market volatility. By spreading investments across various sectors and asset classes, you can mitigate risks associated with overexposure to any single market segment.
Stay Informed: Keeping abreast of market trends and economic indicators can help you make informed decisions. Regularly reviewing financial news and analyses can provide insights into potential market shifts, allowing you to adjust your strategy proactively.
Risk Management: Implementing risk management techniques, such as setting stop-loss orders or rebalancing your portfolio, can help you safeguard against significant losses. These measures act as financial sunscreen, providing a layer of protection against unexpected downturns.
Long-Term Perspective: While it's tempting to react to short-term market movements, maintaining a long-term investment perspective can help you weather temporary fluctuations. Historical data shows that markets tend to recover over time, rewarding patient investors.
Consult Financial Advisors: Professional advisors can offer personalized advice tailored to your financial goals and risk tolerance. They can help you navigate complex market conditions and make adjustments to your portfolio as needed.
Weathering Both Heat Waves
Just as staying hydrated and seeking cool environments are essential during a physical heat wave, staying informed and diversifying your investments are crucial in a heated market. The current climate, both meteorologically and financially, underscores the importance of proactive measures to protect well-being and financial health.
As the heat dome continues to dominate weather patterns in the Midwest and Northeast, remember that preparation and precaution can mitigate its effects. Similarly, as the stock market reaches new heights, strategic planning and risk management can help ensure that your portfolio thrives even under the pressure of record-breaking highs.
Whether it's the intense summer heat or the fiery stock market, both demand a careful and considered approach. By taking steps to shield yourself from the risks associated with these high temperatures, you can enjoy the benefits without suffering the consequences.
This information should not be construed by any client or prospective client as the rendering of personalized investment advice. For more information, please visit BushWealth.com for our full disclosures.

title: School consolidation: Supt. Shirley Joseph makes her recommendation
description: Rick Patrick rick@greenepublishing.com Ahead of an expected final decision by the Madison County District School Board on Monday, July 15, Madison County Superintendent of Schools Shirley Joseph h…
content:
Rick Patrick
rick@greenepublishing.com
Ahead of an expected final decision by the Madison County District School Board on Monday, July 15, Madison County Superintendent of Schools Shirley Joseph has made her recommendation on the topic of school consolidation. The matter of whether or not to keep Greenville Elementary School (GES), Lee Elementary School (LES) and Pinetta Elementary School (PES) open in the face of declining enrollment or to close the schools and bring those students into one school as a cost-saving measure has been open to debate for several years. There have been impassioned arguments made on both sides of the issue.
After hearing the recommendations of Dr. James Brown, of PSTB Consulting, LLC, Supt. Joseph spelled out her plan in a 45-page document which was posted online on the district's web page. It is expected this will be the same document to be presented to the School Board during their meeting on July 15. According to the document, it is recommended to:
• Consolidate any school that has fewer than 250 students enrolled (this is the number of students needed to generate enough state funding to effectively support operations of a school).
• Move all district traditional public school PreK-sixth grade students to Madison County Central School (MCCS).
• Move all district traditional public school grade seven and eight students to Madison County High School (MCHS).
The document states that GES 'has 94 students enrolled and has been near this enrollment level for several years. The prediction at this date by district Student Information Systems (SIS) is that there will be 87 students in [the] 2024-25 school year enrolled per Florida Department of Education (FDOE) Facility Office, this is 41 percent of total capacity. It is a persistently low-performing school that is hard to staff and has constant turnover in staff. The funding the school generates from the state Florida Education Finance Plan (FEFP) for full time equivalent students (FTE) is not enough to sustain the operation of the school, its staff, its resource needs and still operate efficiently. There is no projection that enrollment in the school will improve in the next several years. During community workshops at this school site, staff and families spoke highly of their desire to keep this school open and remain as one community, one family rather than consolidate into the MCCS … It is recommended that the school be closed and the children be relocated to MCCS which is a higher performing school and will be able to offer the students and their parents more resources than are available at GES.'
PES faces a similar picture. The report states that, 'PES has 133 students enrolled and has had consistent falling enrollment levels for the past several years, even after grade six was added back to the school. As of this date, SIS projections for enrollment at PES are at 130 for 2024-25 school year, which includes 10 pre-K students who do not generate FTE. Per FDOE Facility Office, the school is at 59 percent of capacity. PES has been improving academically, but the improvements are being funded due to the additional state funding through Unified School Improvement Grant (UniSIG) that they were able to be awarded because the school was identified by FDOE as a low-performing school. UniSIG funding will not be available in the upcoming school year and there is no revenue source available that can sustain the current level of staffing that is beyond the staffing allocation plan for PES, based on its enrollment. PES is unable to sustain itself at its current level of enrollment with the state funding it generates from FEFP. There is no projection that enrollment at PES would improve over the next several years. Forecasting indicates that enrollment will further decline … It is recommended that the school be closed and the children be relocated to MCCS, which will be able to offer the students and their parents more resources than are available at PES.'
It was stated that LES 'has 170 students enrolled and has had consistently falling enrollments for the past several years, even after grade six was added back to the school. Enrollment projections from SIS for LES are 175 for 2024-25 school year, with 10 students in pre-K that do not generate any FTE funding. Per FDOE Facility Office, LES is at 74 percent of its total capacity. Over the past several years academics have fallen, but there are efforts being made to correct the decline and maintain at least a C accountability grade, which is down from an A grade three years prior. The school is currently overstaffed and has grade levels that are under the state class size limits. This school is hard to staff and operate and has constant turnover in staff positions. The school is unable to sustain itself and its staff and operate efficiently relying just on the state funding it generates from FTE. There is no projection that enrollment in the school would improve in the next several years. Forecasting indicates that enrollment will further decline in the upcoming school years … It is recommended that the school be closed and the children be relocated to MCCS, which will be able to offer the students and their parents more resources than are available at LES.'
It was also recommended that the seventh and eighth grade students be moved from MCCS to MCHS in order to make room for the additional students at MCCS from GES, LES and PES.
One question that has arisen is what to do with the physical buildings currently housing GES, LES and PES, should consolidation take place. There are suggestions made in each case:
• GES would become a Bezos Academy, offering Montessori-based early learning for ages two to five. For more information about Bezos Academies, please visit bezosaucademy.org.
• LES - transfer district administrative staff to the site and reconfigure the site to house all district transportation and maintenance vehicles and accommodate transportation needs for fuel and secure storage; relocate the Credit Union to LES; reconfigure the site to include new Board Room/multipurpose room, staff training center and offices for Board members; oof off site for use as transportation parking and use proceeds for renovations.
• PES - Reconfigure building(s) on site and transform into affordable teacher housing units; reconfigure gym and cafeteria to become a consolidated community center for the housing project.
• District Office - convert to be a central warehouse for all district bulk purchasing; provide housing for all IT/MIS servers and equipment, as well as offices for IT techs; create IT training space for video distance learning projects.
• District Annex - sell building and use proceeds for consolidation renovations and preparations.
Should the School Board take these recommendations, they would not take effect until the 2025-26 school year. In the meantime, the work of transitioning into the consolidation would begin. This would include forming committees consisting of community, school, families and administration working together in order to 'support a positive transition for students, staff and families.'
The full text of the Superintendent's report and recommendations can be found at https://digitalbell-bucket.s3.amazonaws.com/B48CEA4D-F816-827C-D7F7-2FDCC7377230.pdf.
The School Board is expected to take action on the recommendations during the regular meeting of the School Board on Monday, July 15. The meeting is scheduled to begin at 6 p.m. At the current time, the meeting is set to take place in the District Office, located at 210 NE Duval Ave., in Madison.

title: Sugar Cane Festival vendor spots available
description: Heather Ainsley news@greenepublishing.com The annual Sugar Cane Festival, sponsored by Suwannee Hardware and Feed, announced recently that there are a few vendor spots left for the upcoming event.…
content:
Heather Ainsley
news@greenepublishing.com
The annual Sugar Cane Festival, sponsored by Suwannee Hardware and Feed, announced recently that there are a few vendor spots left for the upcoming event.
Don Junior Wilson, the owner of Suwannee Hardware and Feed, announced on Facebook on Friday, June 21, that they are looking to fill a few open vendor spots. This fall's festival will be the Third Annual Sugar Cane Festival. Wilson said the town was looking to do a festival, and chose sugar cane because they wanted something different than common themes like blueberries and strawberries.
The festival, on Friday, Nov. 8 and Saturday, Nov. 9, will have a variety of entertainment, food and shopping for everyone, including live bands, arts and crafts, over 60 vendors, hands-on demonstrations, clogging, a pie eating contest, crowning Mr. and Mrs. Sugar Cane, vintage tractors, hit-miss engines, vintage autos, motorcycles and cruise-ins, a street dance on Friday, Nov. 8, and the Soap Box Derby on Saturday, Nov. 9. The hands-on demonstrations include old fashioned cane grinding, traditional blacksmithing, goat milk soap making, butter churning, honey bee keeping, old fashioned ice cream, yarn spinning, bowl turning, pottery spinning, axe throwing and a chainsaw sculpture artist. Wilson said the vendor who makes the sugar cane syrup makes syrup in advance and makes batches fresh for attendees to watch, and at past festivals, he never left with extra bottles of syrup.
The kids' corner has activities and event for kids to participate in, including a train ride, pony rides, a bounce house and slides, face painting, a petting zoo, a greasy pole climb and a sack race.
The Soap Box Derby allows contestants of all ages to use their creativity to create their cart out of almost anything, according to Wilson. There are three divisions for contestants to enter, based on their age: 8-12 year olds, 13-17 year olds and 18 and up. There is a $25 entree fee for derby participants, and the rules and regulations can be found by emailing suwanneehardware@gmail.com. Wilson said the derby is an event he wanted to do because of the big hill where the festival is held.
'The first one was a great time,' Wilson said. 'A great thing for families to do to build a car together.'
In his post, Wilson said that Suwannee Hardware and Feed is the only contact for vendors, so they know it is a scam if they receive information about being a vendor from anyone else. Interested vendors can email their business information to Wilson at suwanneehardware@gmail.com.

title: Eastern equine encephalitis confirmed in Madison County
description: Rick Patrick rick@greenepublishing.com According to the equimanagement.com web site, a case of the mosquito-borne virus known as Eastern equine encephalitis (EEE) has been confirmed in Madison Cou…
content:
Rick Patrick
rick@greenepublishing.com
According to the equimanagement.com web site, a case of the mosquito-borne virus known as Eastern equine encephalitis (EEE) has been confirmed in Madison County. The web site stated that a two-year-old quarter horse stallion tested positive in late June after the horse developed cellulitis and neurological signs on Thursday, June 20. The horse was subsequently euthanized. Other cases have occurred in Columbia and Holmes Counties.
According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, humans rarely contract EEE. However, when humans do fall ill to the disease, it can be very serious. About 30 percent of people with EEE die, with many of the survivors suffering with ongoing neurologic problems. Symptoms of EEE in humans include fever, headache, vomiting, diarrhea, seizures, behavioral changes and drowsiness. There are no vaccines or medicines to prevent or treat the disease in humans, although there is a vaccine to prevent the disease in horses.
The most effective way of preventing EEE in humans and in horses is to avoid mosquito bites. Some ways to accomplish this include:
• Use insect repellents when outdoors, especially during the dusk and dawn hours when mosquitos are most active.
• Cover or eliminate any containers with standing water, even a teaspoon of water can harbor mosquito eggs.
• Keep horses up to date with an EEE vaccines at least once per year, possibly more often in high-risk areas, such as North Florida.
• If you have water tanks that are at least 18 inches deep, consider stocking them with 'mosquito fish,' which are small fish that love to feed on mosquito larvae.
• Fix or install window and door screens.
• If possible, put horses in stables, stalls or barns during the peak mosquito hours between dusk and dawn.
• Consider obtaining a fogger and use it during the dusk hours when mosquitos are active, but beneficial insects such as bees are not.
EEE is just one of the mosquito-borne diseases that put people at risk. The risk can be greatly reduced by taking preventive measures.

title: Laura's garden notes – Leaning into the heat
description: Laura Young news@greenepublishing.com North Florida in July is hot. Even a brief, early morning session in the garden can turn one into a dripping mess. While perspiration is busy doing its main jo…
content:
Laura Young
news@greenepublishing.com
North Florida in July is hot. Even a brief, early morning session in the garden can turn one into a dripping mess.
While perspiration is busy doing its main job of regulating your body temperature, other important things are going on, too. We have two to four million sweat glands over our skin and all that flow of moisture and oils out to the body's surface can help keep the skin healthy and hydrated.
Sweating also helps the body maintain a balanced pH. Even a slight imbalance of blood pH can make a person feel sick, irritable and uncomfortable; proper blood pH is essential for critical bodily functions like oxygen delivery to tissues, correct protein structure and biochemical reactions essential for life.
What to Plant This Month: If you're willing to be out there sweatily digging and such in July, UF/IFAS has tomato and pepper transplants back on the list after a couple months. If you want to have homegrown tomatoes or peppers this fall, you'll need to plant them this month or in August. July also offers a brief window of time for planting cucumber and pumpkin seeds for fall harvest. Next month, apparently, will be too late.
What's Coming Along: The cucumbers are faring well this year. Last summer, they sprouted like they should and grew a few leaves but then promptly turned yellow and died. This year, despite the recent heat wave (or perhaps because of it), the cucumber plants are vigorously climbing. Cucumbers apparently thrive in the heat, but their soil needs to be kept moist.
What we're eating in July: Juicy tomatoes have a regular place on plates in July, along with a steady supply of crisp banana peppers and dark zucchini.
Potatoes sometimes get a thumbs down from a nutritional standpoint, but they actually have many benefits. Notably, potatoes have more potassium than bananas, and this mineral is essential for nerves and muscles to function well. Potatoes offer other important minerals, too, like manganese, copper and iron, along with vitamins B6 and C. People who are watching their blood sugar may find blue/purple potatoes a better choice than white or yellow ones. They have a much lower glycemic index along with a high concentration of polyphenol compounds, which may decrease the absorption of starches during digestion. Plus, blue/purple potatoes are really high in antioxidants called anthocyanins that reduce the risk of several scary diseases while contributing to healthier cholesterol levels and improved eye health.
What's Tempting Me: One way a gardener can lean into the July heat is to solarize areas that are not in production. A UF/IFAS article on the subject explains that solarization involves heating soil under clear plastic, usually for about six weeks or more in order to manage problems like weeds, nematodes and soil-borne diseases.
Solarization can be done in a just a few steps. Clear the area to be solarized, add organic matter if you like, level the dirt and water it well or wait for a good soaking rain. Lay the plastic sheeting down and bury the edges or pin them down with old lumber to keep air from circulating (and cooling) under the plastic. After six to eight weeks, remove the plastic and begin your fall planting.

title: Fatal crash on Interstate 10 diverts traffic
description: Rick Patrick rick@greenepublishing.com According to a report from the Florida Highway Patrol, on Tuesday, July 9, at approximately 1:28 a.m., a single-vehicle crash claimed the life of an Alabama …
content:
Rick Patrick
rick@greenepublishing.com
According to a report from the Florida Highway Patrol, on Tuesday, July 9, at approximately 1:28 a.m., a single-vehicle crash claimed the life of an Alabama man. The crash occurred on the westbound side of Interstate 10 (I-10), near mile marker 251, in Madison County. The report states that a pickup truck, driven by a 56-year-old Anniston, Ala. man was traveling westbound on I-10, near mile marker 251, with a boat and trailer in tow. For unknown reasons, the driver traveled off the roadway to the right and onto the paved shoulder. The truck reentered the travel lanes, at which time the boat and trailer jackknifed. The truck traveled across the travel lanes, and into the center median, where the truck overturned before hitting a guardrail. The truck came to a final rest, overturned in the center median. The westbound lanes of I-10 were shut down, and traffic was diverted off the 251 exit ramp.
Madison County Fire Rescue units responded to the scene, where the driver was pronounced deceased.

title: Cowboys help lead team in World Series tournament
description: Rick Patrick rick@greenepublishing.com The Diamond Kings Sports Academy (DKSA) program may be based out of Thomasville, Ga., but the DKSA Elite 15U team has a pair of players who proudly wear maro…
content:
Rick Patrick
rick@greenepublishing.com
The Diamond Kings Sports Academy (DKSA) program may be based out of Thomasville, Ga., but the DKSA Elite 15U team has a pair of players who proudly wear maroon and silver during the school year. Players Brett Harper and Myron Mobley are both of Madison, although the town's ties with the DKSA program go beyond the players on the team. The team's head coach is Michael Mobley, a long-time baseball coach in Madison.
The DKSA Elite 15U team recently competed in the 2D Sports World Series tournament in Nashville, Tenn. Out of 20 elite travel baseball teams, from as far away as Mississippi and North Carolina, the DKSA Elite 15U team placed third.
The DKSA team dropped the first game of the tournament, 5-2, against Bueprint Baseball 15U, on Wednesday, July 10. Then, on Thursday, July 11, the DKSA players bounced back with a 5-1 victory over the EBC 15U-Fesmire team, a game in which Harper was named the Player of the Game after going one-for-two in the batter's box. Next up for DKSA was an 8-0 shutout win over US Elite Caster 15U. On Saturday, July 13, DKSA continued to put up wins, with a big 12-7 victory over the Wow Factor OHV American 15U team. On Sunday, July 14, the DKSA team won the first half of the day's double-header with a 7-1 win over PYT 15U. The tournament ended for DKSA with a tough 2-4 defeat at the hands of BC Athletics 2027 Carrier 15U.
The DKSA program has the mission of providing 'quality baseball and softball instruction and a competitive training environment for kids of all ages and skill levels for South Georgia and the Big Bend Area.' The program also strives to 'educate athletes on the process and everyday work involved in being a student-athlete and emphasize the importance of academics.'
More information about the DKSA program can be found at www.dksportsacademy.com.

title: Ivy Joy Kelley
description: Ivy Joy Kelley, age 73, died Monday, July 22, 2024, at her home in Madison, Fla. Ivy was born on August 5, 1950, in Fernandina Beach, Fla. She loved to spend time with family and friends, and enjo…
content:
Ivy Joy Kelley, age 73, died Monday, July 22, 2024, at her home in Madison, Fla.
Ivy was born on August 5, 1950, in Fernandina Beach, Fla.
She loved to spend time with family and friends, and enjoyed the outdoors, hunting and fishing. If you didn't catch her in a boat with her husband, Mike, fishing or in the woods hunting deer, you could likely see her at a convenience store playing scratch off lottery tickets or at an internet coffee casino.
She was predeceased by her parents, Howard and Iris Robinson; brothers, Roger and Gary Robinson; sister, Barbara Merritt; son, Darron Coody; and grandson, Christopher Sapp.
She is survived by her husband, Mike Kelley, of Madison, Fla.; brother, Jackie Robinson (Cathy), of Ocala, Fla.; son, Allen Coody, of Pinetta, Fla.; stepson, William Kelley; stepdaughter, Bobbi Sapp; grandchildren: J. D. Coody, Shane Coody, Hope McCool (Brandon), Hunter Kelley, Lincoln Kelley, Caleb Sapp and Ashton Sapp; as well as a host of nieces and nephews.

title: Local Badcock stores to undergo major rebranding
description: Alexa Duarte reporter2.riverbendnews@gmail.com Rumors around town and on social media have been about the local Badcock stores and if they will be closing. Riverbend News has been in contact with l…
content:
Alexa Duarte
reporter2.riverbendnews@gmail.com
Rumors around town and on social media have been about the local Badcock stores and if they will be closing. Riverbend News has been in contact with local Badcock owners since these rumors started. Parent company, Conn's filed for bankruptcy last week and they purchased Badcock back in December. The stores will not be closing by any means but only going through a process of rebranding to stay under the Badcock name or changing the name.
An inventory liquidation sale started on Thursday, July 25, and will run until Thursday, October 31, so that the old merchandise will go out to bring in new merchandise. Sale prices will begin from anywhere from 30 percent to 50 percent. The company is very excited to begin this new journey and looks forward to helping provide for the community with its same excellent customer service.
Steven Anderson, area Badcock manger, said 'The Badcock stores are looking forward to not being affiliated with the Conn's Company and to be able to go to the same Badcock that people have known and loved for many years.'
Regarding the future name of Badcock, Anderson stated he isn't sure if the name will stay the same, but the location and staff will remain the same.

title: Florida driver's license numbers changing

content:

In an effort to help better protect personal information, numbers on Florida Driver's Licenses will be changing, effective Wednesday, July 31. Those seeking a new, renewed or replacement license will be issued a randomly-generated number to replace the old number. This change is required by Florida State Legislature Senate Bill 914, which was passed in 2022. At this point, drivers do not need to make any special arrangements for a new license. The changes will take place as current licenses come up for renewal or need to be replaced.
When new license numbers are given, people should be sure to notify employers, financial institutions, insurance companies, etc. of the new number.
Information about driver's license renewals can be found through the Madison County Tax Collector's Office, located at 229 SW Pinckney St., Room 102, in Madison. The phone number is (850) 973-6136. You may also visit the Madison County Tax Collector's website at https://madisontc.com.

title: Remembering Madison's finer moments in film
description: Mickey Starling reporter3@greenepublishing.com Madison County is most often remembered for its natural beauty, small-town charm and more than a few antique shops. But, on a few occasions, a bright…
content:
Mickey Starling
reporter3@greenepublishing.com
Madison County is most often remembered for its natural beauty, small-town charm and more than a few antique shops. But, on a few occasions, a brighter spotlight has shined upon our community as film makers have chosen to produce movies in our fair hamlet.
In 1990, producers made use of Blue Springs in the filming of 'The Spring', featuring Buck Christmas and other locals as they make a dash for Ponce de Leon's fountain of youth. The movie depicts the discovery of the fabled fountain and the conflicts that arise with some unsavory folks trying to profit from it. Unfortunately, watching the locals is the best part of this otherwise lackluster production.
A better-quality film made it's way to the Madison County Courthouse in 2016, when 'Prayer Never Fails' was produced. This faith-based movie starred Nick Lashaway, Lorenzo Lamas, Corbin Bernsen and Clifton Davis. The movie tells the story of a high school coach who confronts the principal for taking funds from the athletic program. The principal soon fires him for praying with an ailing student. The conflict escalates, eventually landing in a courtroom. Other important topics, such as abuse and addiction are also covered, and the power of prayer is emphasized throughout the difficult circumstances that the characters face.
'Prayer Never Fails' received impressive reviews from sites such as movieguide.org for its strong content and ability to deal with difficult issues in a believable manner. Genuine struggles with faith are not hidden but shown as part of the journey towards redemption. 'Prayer Never Fails' is available for free on numerous popular streaming services, including Amazon Prime, iTunes and many others.

title: Governor vetoes vacation rental bill that sought to strip local control of industry
description: Lazaro Aleman news@greenepublishing.com Score a small victory for city and county governments, which recently found themselves on the winning side of a governor veto relative to a bill that sought…
content:
Lazaro Aleman
news@greenepublishing.com
Score a small victory for city and county governments, which recently found themselves on the winning side of a governor veto relative to a bill that sought to wrest local control of vacation rental properties and give it to the state.
Senate Bill 280, which Gov. Ron DeSantis vetoed on Thursday, June 27, would have eliminated all local regulation of vacation rental properties and turned that authority to the state. Under the bill, local governments would still have had the ability to respond to noise and safety concerns involving vacation properties, but they would have been stripped of all regulatory ordinances implemented since 2016.
In his veto letter, DeSantis wrote that the proposed legislation would create new bureaucratic red tape that would prevent local governments from enforcing existing ordinances or passing any new measures that applied exclusively to vacation rentals.
'Under the bill,' DeSantis wrote, 'any such measure must apply to all residential properties. The effect of this provision will prevent virtually all local regulation of vacation rental even though the vacation rental markets are far from uniform across the various regions of the state.'
The governor noted that going forward, he encouraged the legislators and key stakeholders to work together 'with the understanding that vacation rentals should not be approached as a one-size-fits-all issue.'
The governor's action was seen as a rarity in an administration that has increasingly acted to enhance state authority at the expense of local governments.
It is also indicative of the extremely controversial nature of the measure, which reportedly struggled to pass in both chambers, despite Republicans having a supermajority in the Legislature and Senate President Kathleen Passidomo championing the legislation. The vacation rental properties bill drew strong opposition from local governments across the state, as well as from vacation rental management companies and the Florida Association of Realtors.
While popular among a segment of property owners as a ready source of income, especially in the state's coastal communities, others see vacation rental properties as causing disruptions to neighborhoods, reducing affordable housing and lowering property values.

August is National Breastfeeding Month (NBM), with the 2024 NBM Theme being: Nourish, Sustain, Thrive.
The 2024 theme will share the importance of protecting, promoting and supporting lactation. World Breastfeeding Week (WBW) was created in 1992 by the World Alliance for Breastfeeding Action (WABA) and is celebrated annually from Aug. 1 to Aug. 7. Since 2016, the WABA has aligned their WBW campaign to the United Nation's Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs).
In August, every week will highlight and celebrate different groups, showing the importance of lactation and promoting support to all. Here are the different themes throughout the week:
• World Breastfeeding Week -Closing the Gap: Thursday, Aug. 1, through Wednesday, Aug. 7.
• Indigenous Milk Medicine Week: Thursday, Aug. 8, through Wednesday, Aug. 14.
• Asian American, Native Hawaiian and Pacific Islander Breastfeeding Week: Thursday, Aug. 15, through Wednesday, Aug. 21.
• Black Breastfeeding Week: Sunday, Aug. 25, through Saturday, Aug. 31.

title: Bart Alford – Candidate for Superintendent of Schools
description: My name is Bart Alford, and I am seeking the office of Superintendent of Schools for Madison County. I understand the challenges and accountability that come with this office. My experience as a sc…
content:
My name is Bart Alford, and I am seeking the office of Superintendent of Schools for Madison County. I understand the challenges and accountability that come with this office. My experience as a school board member and my work in the classroom has prepared me with the leadership skills and the institutional knowledge necessary to guide the district. Every student in our county deserves a high-quality education, and our moral obligation as a district is to provide it. Continuous growth in the school district will occur through a systematic plan focusing on transforming teaching and learning, where all students demonstrate academic growth and achievement.
I served on the school board for 20 years (2002-2022). I worked with five superintendents and served as chairman for six years. I received Master Board training twice and held the distinction of Certified School Board Member from the Florida School Board Association.
Before joining the school board, I worked as a speech-language pathologist in Madison and Jefferson County School District. I worked with regular and special education students from pre-k through the high school level. I served students at various schools in Madison and Monticello. Currently, I work at Taylor County Elementary School in Perry, Florida, where I was named "Teacher of the Year" in 2022.
I graduated from Madison County High School, North Florida Junior College, and Florida State University. From Florida State University, I received both my bachelor's and master's degrees in speech-language pathology. I hold licensure as a speech-language pathologist through the State of Florida and national certification through the American Speech-Language-Hearing Association (ASHA).
Over the past two decades, I have been active in the school system and community, with a solid commitment to Madison County's students and teachers.
I am passionate about the opportunity to lead the transformation in instructional methods to improve student learning and mastery of content in the classroom. As a district, we must ensure the curriculum I presented rigorously, creatively, and with fidelity to enhance student engagement, a soon-to-be hallmark of each grade level. A strong emphasis will continue with literacy, and we must strive to increase the number of students proficient in reading and math by the end of first grade. A student should be reading at grade level in the second grade. In all practicality, if a student is not at grade level by the third grade, the learning gap is often so significant they never catch up, increasing their likelihood of not finishing high school. The school district will target improving reading and math skills at all levels, catalyzing the district's transformational reform. To improve the proficiency level of all students, we will focus on enhancing tier-one instruction in the classroom, expanding remediation services in math and reading, and participating in the Accelerated Reading program, which will be mandatory for all students. All employees with an active teaching certificate not currently in the classroom will provide daily small-group instruction for struggling students. Moving all students to achieve expected learning gains and proficiency levels is essential. We will accomplish this improvement through innovative teaching and scheduling methods.
I am dedicated to advancing our district to the next level of academic achievement, while creating a district that attracts students. We must work to ensure that academic excellence is a dream and a reality for all students. I accept the challenge of this office and look forward to the opportunity to lead our district as we continue to raise the bar of excellence. I appreciate your consideration and vote as you vote for the next Superintendent of Schools for Madison County.
Question 1. There have been complaints about the public schools food being expired, moldy, and unfit for a child to eat how will you ensure our children are getting healthy and nutritious food at school.
Answer: All the public schools in the Madison County School District offer free breakfast and lunch to all students. We live in a poor community and food insecurities are real and many children depend on the meals they receive daily at school to meet their nutritional needs. I will do everything in my power to ensure that students continue to receive nutritious meals. I can say the food service department, under the supervision of Iris Wynn, meets the children's nutritional needs with both breakfast and lunch meals. If molded or outdated food was served, it was served unknowingly and was corrected immediately when discovered. The food Service department is governed by the Florida Department of Agriculture and Consumer Services. The kitchens in the district are pristine in cleanliness and organization. I also had meals prepared by the kitchen staff at school functions and they were good meals. The district and food service department will continue to follow the required nutritional guidelines and any complaints will be investigated and improved upon when needed.
Question 2. How are you going to enforce stricter policies on the bullying, harassment and threats taking place at schools weekly?
Answer: I will not tolerate bullying, harassment and threats taking place in the school setting among students. Students will behave in class and throughout the school day, or have consequences based on the board-approved code of student conduct. The Madison County School Board currently has explicit and detailed policies on bullying and harassment in the code of conduct. It is not that we need stricter policies but to show the students that misbehavior will not be tolerated, and punishment will follow such actions. Students have a right to be safe at school, and I will work with school administrators to ensure students are safe while bullying, harassment and threats are not tolerated. I am open to reviewing the policy if additions are needed. When students are instructed in a structured, engaging learning environment with supervision during transitions and special areas, they are less likely to be bullied or harassed during the school day. Students are at school to learn, and I refuse to allow students to abuse innocent students through bullying, harassment, and threats.
Question 3. How do you see the community, specifically our school system, in 5 years and what would you do in your office to achieve that vision, should you be elected?
Answer: In the next five years, I see improvements in reading and math proficiency for struggling students while average and above-average students will be pushed to reach their full potential academically. The academic improvement will occur due to the curriculum being presented rigorously, creatively, and with fidelity. A strong emphasis will be placed on literacy and the number of students proficient in reading by the end of the first grade will increase. The school district will target improving reading and math skills at all levels. The district will focus on improving tier-one instruction in the classroom, expanding remediation services in math and reading, and participating in a mandatory Accelerated Reading program. All employees with an active teaching certificate not in the classroom will provide daily small-group instruction for students. These efforts will help all students achieve expected learning gains and proficiency levels.
