rick@greenepublishing.com
The Florida Department of Education (DOE) has released their grades for school districts and individual schools across the Sunshine State. The Madison County School District again received a 'C' grade, which is the same grade received since 2019. In 2018, the district did receive a grade of 'B.'
According to the DOE, 'a school's grade may include up to twelve components. There are five achievement components and four learning gains components, as well as components for middle school acceleration, graduation rate and college and career acceleration. Each component is worth up to 100 points in the overall calculation.' Points are awarded based on performance in these components. The school's grade is calculated by adding the number of points earned for each component and dividing that number by the total number of points available in order to arrive at a percentage of points earned. The grading scale for elementary schools is: A = 62 percent of points or greater, B = 54 percent to 61 percent, C = 41 percent to 53 percent, D = 32 percent to 40 percent and F = 31 percent of points or less. The grading scale for middle, high and combination schools is: A = 64 percent of points or greater, B = 57 percent to 63 percent of points, C = 44 percent to 56 percent of points, D = 34 percent to 43 percent and F = 33 percent of points or less.
In terms of individual schools, Madison County High School (MCHS) received an 'I.' In order to receive a grade, at least 95 percent of students must have been tested. The percentage of students tested at MCHS was not released in the report. Madison County Central School received a 'C,' with 49 percent of total possible points earned. Greenville Elementary School received an 'F' grade, with 31 percent of the total possible points earned. Lee Elementary School received a 'C' grade for earning 50 percent of the total possible points. Pinetta Elementary School received a 'C' grade with 48 percent of total possible points earned. James Madison Preparatory School received a 'C' grade for 52 percent of total possible points. Madison Creative Arts Academy received an 'A' grade earning 64 percent of possible points.
According to the DOE, statewide, schools have shown improvement with 64 percent of all schools earning a grade a 'A or 'B,' compared to 57 percent of schools in 2023. Less than four percent of schools earned a 'D' or 'F' in 2024, compared to six percent of schools in 2023. A total of 1,761 schools, or 53 percent, either improved their grade or maintained an 'A' in 2024.
Greene Publishing, Inc. reached out to Madison County Superintendent of Schools Shirley Joseph for a comment. However, as of press time, no response has been received.
Information on all schools and school districts can be found at https://www.fldoe.org/accountability/accountability-reporting/school-grades/.

title: A final salute

content:

The gymnasium on the Madison County High School (MCHS) campus was not filled with the usual cheers of an exciting Cowboys basketball game on Thursday, July 18. Instead, it carried the sound of a somber silence as the men and women of the Madison County Sheriff's Office (MCSO) honored fallen K9 Archer with a touching memorial service. Law enforcement officers and other first responders from across the state gathered to pay their final respects to the K9 who tragically passed away in the line of duty.
Deputy K9 Archer was a German shepherd, born on Oct. 8, 2017, in the Czech Republic. He began his service to the MCSO in September of 2018, just before his first birthday. Archer gained national certification in numerous areas, including tracking, narcotics detection and, most importantly, handler protection. Archer was credited with several felony apprehensions, as well as helping to rid the streets of Madison County of dangerous narcotics on many occasions. Archer was also a beloved ambassador for the MCSO, participating in many demonstrations for youngsters and adults alike.
During the service, MCSO Sheriff David Harper gave a touching recitation of the poem, 'K9 Promise.'
My eyes are your eyes,
To watch and protect you and yours.
My ears are your ears,
To hear and detect evil minds in the dark.
My nose is your nose,
To scent the invader of your domain.
And so you may live,
My life is also yours.
Author - Unknown
Deputy K9 Archer, end of watch July 5, 2024.

title: Ground broken on new fire station
description: Rick Patrick rick@greenepublishing.com Thanks to $850,000 in funding from the Florida legislature, Madison County will have a new fire station on Dale Leslie Drive, near Lee, close to Interstate 1…
content:
Rick Patrick
rick@greenepublishing.com
Thanks to $850,000 in funding from the Florida legislature, Madison County will have a new fire station on Dale Leslie Drive, near Lee, close to Interstate 10. On Wednesday, July 24, a ground-breaking ceremony was held to commemorate the beginning of construction for the new station. The ceremony was attended by several community and state leaders, including the legislative delegation of Rep. Allison Tant and State Sen. Corey Simon, who represent Madison County.
'We are very grateful to both Rep. Tant and Sen. Simon for their help in making this happen,' said Madison County Fire Rescue Chief, Allen Clayton. 'This will help reduce call times and help save lives.'
Public safety is one of the most important things for us,' said Sen. Simon. 'Every time we see one of these ground-breaking ceremonies, that represents progress for this district and the community.'
'Nearly 30 percent of the calls for help come from this part of Madison,' said Rep. Tant. 'Having a fire station here will cut response time in half, or more, resulting in saving lives and property. I'm honored to do this for my constituents.'
The need for this station was illustrated when a call came through the radio near the end of the ceremony. Several responders hopped into a truck and headed to the call on South State Road 53, not far from where the new station will be located.
The new station is expected to be completed sometime in the spring of 2025.

title: Florida's population passes 23 million
description: Leah Androski reporter@greenepublishing.com Florida's population crossed the 23 million mark due to the increased number of people moving from other states. As of April 1 of this year, Florida had…
content:
Leah Androski
reporter@greenepublishing.com
Florida's population crossed the 23 million mark due to the increased number of people moving from other states.
As of April 1 of this year, Florida had 29,002,597 residents, according to estimates released by the state Demographic Estimating Conference. Florida trails behind California's 39.5 million and Texas' 30.5 million as the third most populous state. This peak is expected to get smaller yearly as the number of baby boomers entering retirement gets smaller. Florida's growth rate will be under one percent, by the early 2030s, after hitting 1.6 percent this year.
Due to this statistic, deaths have outpaced births in Florida since late 2019, this trend is expected continue into the next decade. Almost 10 percent of Florida's residents are age 75 and older, second only to Puerto Rico among U.S. states and the territory.

title: Cowboys attend Fellowship of Christian Athletes camp
description: Rick Patrick rick@greenepublishing.com A total of 43 young men from the Madison County High School (MCHS) Cowboys football team recently attended the Fellowship of Christian Athletes football camp…
content:
Rick Patrick
rick@greenepublishing.com
A total of 43 young men from the Madison County High School (MCHS) Cowboys football team recently attended the Fellowship of Christian Athletes football camp in Lakeland, Fla. While at the camp, from Monday, July 22, through Wednesday, July 24, the young athletes were able to compete with other teams from across the state in 'thud' scrimmage competition. A thud scrimmage carries some contact, but not as much as in a regular game. During a thud scrimmage, contact is targeted to the upper body and ball carriers are 'wrapped up,' but not taken to the ground. Naturally, there is much less risk of injury during these types of scrimmages.
According to MCHS Head Coach Price Harris, perhaps the greatest value in participation in the camp is not what happens on the gridiron. During the camp, the participants take part in various activities led by camp staff that help build unity and brotherhood among the players. They also hear from various speakers who speak about character and life decisions that will have an impact on their life successes, well beyond their high school years.
'One of the most important things emphasized by the coaching staff is that life is about more than football,' said Coach Harris. 'Football is not who we are, it is what we do. The players' value is in who they are, not in how they play. Finding balance between being competitive (the will to win) and having character is something we strive to find. I was very proud of how they represented Madison County, their families and our team. The kids had an opportunity to see it is bigger than them. What are they willing to do? Are they willing to 'Hold the Line?''
The MCHS Cowboys will begin a tough and grueling 2024 campaign with their annual Kickoff Classic pre-season game against the War Eagles of Wakulla High School, on Friday, Aug. 16. Kickoff is scheduled to take place at 7:30 p.m., at Boot Hill Stadium. The Cowboys' regular season starts on the road against the Bulldogs of DeLand High School on Friday, Aug. 23, at 7:30 p.m.

title: Jamie Andrews – Candidate for School Board District 2
description: I graduated from VSU in 1999 with a degree in Early Childhood Education and immediately began my teaching career. This year marked my 25th year in the classroom. I have been married to my husband, …
content:
I graduated from VSU in 1999 with a degree in Early Childhood Education and immediately began my teaching career. This year marked my 25th year in the classroom.
I have been married to my husband, Billy Andrews, for 25 years, and we have one daughter, Kylie.
As an active classroom educator, I have a unique perspective on the current challenges facing our schools and classrooms. I also have strong relationships with our current school administrators and many of our county teachers, making them comfortable approaching me with the issues our schools are facing.
I taught in Madison County schools for 18 years until this year when I switched districts to gain new knowledge and ideas to bring back to our district as I planned my run for School Board Representative. This experience gives me unique insight into the strengths and weaknesses of different educational environments.
Even while teaching in a new district, I have remained available to Madison County school administrators and teachers. I frequently volunteer at school functions and attend school celebrations to cheer on and support our Madison County students.
During my time in the Madison County school district, I served as a teacher mentor, a union representative, and a member of the bargaining committee for negotiations between the district and staff.
I have also been involved with a local service organization in Madison County for the past 15 years. Through this organization, I have helped organize food bags for families with food insecurities, put books in the hands of our children, delivered holiday meals to families, and granted Christmas wishes for local children.
As a Madison County teacher, I regularly assisted colleagues in securing supplies for their students through grant writing and helped the district receive a truckload of disinfecting wipes through the Frontline Impact Grant to help keep our schools clean and ease the financial burden of purchasing these supplies.
In recognition of my efforts, I was honored by Ellen DeGeneres in 2020, received the Teacher of the Month award from WCTV in 2021, and was nominated for a Life Changer of the Year award in 2022.
I have a deep love for Madison County and our families and am confident that I can make a meaningful difference in our schools by serving on the Madison County School Board.
Nutrition in Our Schools
Let me start by saying that I know Mrs. Iris Wynn and I haven't seen where this is currently a problem in our district. I have eaten many cafeteria meals and even planned my days off to make sure I didn't miss the baked chicken. I'm confident our district is doing a good job training cafeteria staff on preparing and serving nutritious meals and educating them about the importance of sticking to nutrition standards.
I'd like to see us make our nutrition programs more comprehensive by including them in the PE curriculum. In the past, the Health department has brought in a nutritional expert to teach lessons a few times a month, which has been great.
Although inexperienced in the area, I'm also open to the idea of partnering with local farms where they could come in and educate our students on where their food comes from, as many of our students are unaware.. Of course, this won't happen overnight, and we'd need to look into funding and grants, like farm-to-school grants or other federal and state opportunities, to make it possible. We used to receive various fruits and vegetables as snacks for our students in the afternoons and I'd like to see if this is a possibility in the future.
From my experience our staff are competent at ensuring school meals accommodate various dietary needs, including allergies, religious restrictions, and cultural preferences, with documentation from guardians.
I would, however, I'd like us to offer more choices that appeal to different age groups to ensure every child leaves school full, especially since many of our students may experience food insecurities. With all of this in mind, we need to be conscious of the budget before moving forward with new initiatives.
Bullying and Prevention
Enforcing stricter policies on bullying, harassment, and threats in schools is key to creating a safe and supportive environment for everyone.
First, we need to make sure our district has clear, detailed anti-bullying policies that clearly define what bullying, harassment, and threats are, including cyberbullying. These policies should be age-appropriate and communicated effectively to students, staff, and parents. We have had recent policy updates which I am pleased with. We should also establish consistent consequences for any violations, making sure they're fair and proportional to the behavior. It's important that everyone in the school community knows about these consequences. Plus, we should provide support for our staff and families dealing with these issues.
I'd also like to see ongoing training for teachers, staff, and administrators on how to identify, prevent, and respond to bullying and harassment. Maybe we could set up a specific team for this topic so other staff can focus on their areas. This training should include ways to support victims and address the behavior of those who bully.
Implementing age-appropriate bullying prevention programs is crucial. These programs should teach students about empathy, respect, and how to resolve conflicts effectively. We've had Social Emotional Learning lessons in the past, but I think it might be better to integrate them into daily check-ins and morning meetings to make things easier for our staff and give students more opportunities to connect.
Make sure our counselors and support staff are trained to help students who are victims of bullying and those who show bullying behavior. We should also provide access to mental health resources and peer support groups.
We need confidential reporting systems, where students can report bullying, harassment, and threats without fear of retaliation. These reports should be taken seriously.
Let's hold workshops and meetings, with incentives, for parents to teach them how to recognize the signs of bullying and how they can support their kids and work with the school to prevent it.
Partnering with local organizations, law enforcement, and mental health professionals can boost our anti-bullying efforts. Community support can give us extra resources and help for students and families. We have had an influx of amazing volunteers thanks to the effort of PTO at MCCS and I believe these would provide great mentor opportunities for those students who need extra support.
In today's world, it's also crucial to teach students about responsible online behavior and the consequences of cyberbullying. We should keep getting feedback through climate surveys to see what's working and what's not so we can make adjustments as needed.
Our schools do a great job of recognizing and rewarding positive behavior and acts of kindness through PBIS activities and celebrations. I'd love to see more funding to support these efforts.
Five Year Plan
As a candidate for school board member, I believe our district has tremendous potential over the next five years, and I'm excited to share my vision for where we could be.
I would love for our district to be a district where our students have access to a wide range of programs during the school day. We could expand offerings to include art, music, agriculture, drama, computers, and certification programs that students can start as early as the 6th grade. These programs would not only spark students' interest but could also help improve attendance because they'd be more engaged and excited about coming to school.
I would like changes to occur that put us in a position to attract and retain top-notch teachers and staff by offering competitive pay and benefits. More importantly, we need to create positive work environments where educators feel valued and supported. Happy, motivated teachers are crucial for our students' success, and recruiting the best talent ensures our students get the high-quality education they deserve. This also means having smaller class sizes and providing adequate planning and prep times for teachers, so they can deliver the best instruction possible.
For our most vulnerable students, we need to address critical shortages in areas like Exceptional Student Education (ESE). We should provide supplements and support so that our ESE teachers have fewer students per caseload and can give more attention to each student's specific needs. This will allow students who can work in peer environments to do so with tremendous support, while those who need a more structured, contained environment can receive services in well-supplied classrooms.
We also need more support and transparency within our district, ensuring that all our staff members—from district to school and community levels—understand and support each other's needs. If we ensure that our students are our first priority, everything else should fall into place. I envision a district where parents and community members are eagerly involved in both curricular and extracurricular activities. The support of the community will make our students feel truly valued and strengthen the bond between schools and the community.
Additionally, I hope that the move towards school consolidation opens up these opportunities for our students. By consolidating, we can pool our resources more effectively, provide a richer variety of programs, and create a more vibrant and supportive learning environment.
In five years, with these initiatives in place, I see our district thriving—a place where students are eager to learn, teachers are excited to teach, and the whole community is proud to be a part of.
Conclusion
My current school calendar provides me with ample time to visit schools and engage directly with students, teachers, and staff, ensuring I remain connected and responsive to their needs. My full-time job does not hinder my ability to be actively involved in school activities; rather, it keeps me fully aware of the problems and issues our schools and staff face, enabling me to dedicate the necessary time and energy to serve our community effectively.
Our School Board policy states that The county shall be divided into five (5) residence areas approximately equal in population.Members of the School Board shall be elected by the residents of that member's residence area and once elected shall represent the entire District. I am committed to representing every child, every teacher, every staff member, and every family in our district.
Together, we can create a brighter future for our district. I humbly ask for your support and your vote. Thank you.

title: Children's Eye Health and Safety Month observed
description: Leah Androski reporter@greenepublishing.com Children's Eye Health and Safety Month is observed in August. Without early detection and treatment, uncorrected vision disorders in children can impair …
content:
Leah Androski
reporter@greenepublishing.com
Children's Eye Health and Safety Month is observed in August. Without early detection and treatment, uncorrected vision disorders in children can impair healthy development, interfere with learning and may lead to permanent vision loss.
Some common pediatric eye conditions may include: Astigmatism, Myopia (nearsightedness), Hyperopia (farsightedness), Ptosis (droopy eyelids), Conjunctivitis (pinkeye), Styes, Chalazions, Pediatric Glaucoma, Pediatric Cataracts, Double Vision, Nystagmus, Epiphora (excessive tearing) and blocked tear ducts. Children may also have genetic eye conditions, which may not be apparent at birth.
About 90 percent of eye injuries can be prevented through the use of proper protective eyewear. Here are some habits to adapt around your children to help keep their eyes safe:
• holding sharp objects, such as scissors, away from the face
• using paper clips, rubber bands, safety pins and other objects in ways that do not put eyes at risk
• locking kitchen knives away
• storing cleaning chemicals and hazardous materials away from children
• storing glassware, ceramics and other breakables safely out of reach
• storing guns— including those used for paintball, pellets and BBs— separate from their ammo
• wearing protective eyewear when doing yard work, performing repairs around the house, using power tools, woodworking, swimming or playing sports
• wearing sunglasses outside to prevent UV damage
• wearing protective eyewear during science experiments
• only pet domestic animals with permission from owners
• purchase age-appropriate toys without sharp edges or accessories
• pad sharp corners on furniture
• set gates at top and bottom of staircases
• take breaks when using computer, TV and smartphone screens for long periods of time.

content:
Roy Franklin Milliron, Jr., a beloved husband, father, grandfather and friend, passed away peacefully on Saturday, Aug. 3, 2024, at the age of 83. He was born on June 22, 1941, in Tallahassee, Fla., to Roy Franklin Milliron, Sr. and Myrtle Bevis Milliron, but spent his life in Madison, Fla.
Roy was a member of First Baptist Church of Madison and was a proud graduate of Madison High School and North Florida Junior College. He also attended Florida State University and participated in the FSU Flying High Circus. After a period of serving as the Recreation Director and then the Assistant City Manager in New Port Richey, Fla., he moved back to his hometown of Madison, where he ran a successful real estate business for 30 years. He was dedicated to the community and served as a school board member, two times as Rotary Club President, Economic Development Director and twice as President of Madison County Chamber Of Commerce. He was instrumental in leading the Rail to Trails bike/walking path in Madison County, obtained the signage and dedication for the 100 mile bike loop throughout the county bringing cycling tourism to the county and successfully led the fight to preserve Madison's beautiful natural resources by defeating the location of a hazardous waste incinerator within the County.
Roy's life was characterized by his unwavering love for his family, his devotion to friends and his passion for adventure. An avid outdoorsman, he enjoyed hunting, fishing, hang-gliding, running, cycling, skiing and playing hearts at the campsite. He also loved to travel, taking multiple cross-country trips on a motorcycle. His hobby was woodworking where he created beautiful pieces of art that will be cherished by family and friends for generations to come.
He is survived by his loving wife of 61 years, Suzanne Milliron; his three children and two daughter-in-laws: Scott (Patty) Milliron, of Sanford, Fla., Paige Kelly, of Madison, Fla. and Victor (Shehla) Milliron, of Tallahassee, Fla.; his five grandchildren: Liz, Tyler, Matt, Mary and Kylie; as well as six great-grandchildren: Jace, Bo, Coltin, Kayden, Karson and Hudson.
Roy was preceded in death by his parents and his sister, Laura Coleman.
Roy will be remembered for his example of hard work, quiet strength, honesty and his dedication and love to family, friends and community, along with bringing a laugh to those around him. His legacy lives on through the love and memories he leaves with his family and friends.
Rest in peace, Roy. You will be dearly missed and forever remembered.
A memorial service will be held Saturday, Sept. 14, at 11 a.m., at First Baptist Church 1898 Sanctuary, located at 134 SW Meeting Ave., in Madison.
For any questions, please call Beggs Funeral Home – Madison Chapel at (850) 973-2258. Condolences may be left at beggsfuneral.com.

title: Arrest made in animal cruelty case
description: Madison County Sheriff's Office Contributor Madison County Sheriff David Harper reports the conclusion of an investigation conducted by his Animal Services Division within the Madison County Sheri…
content:
Madison County Sheriff's Office
Contributor
Madison County Sheriff David Harper reports the conclusion of an investigation conducted by his Animal Services Division within the Madison County Sheriff's Office (MCSO). On Wednesday, Sept. 18, Investigators of the MCSO, assisted by Animal Services Officers conducted a search warrant at the home of Matthew Donalies, located at 610 SE Askew Ave., in Madison. The search warrant was the result of an investigation into animal cruelty and neglect and the deplorable conditions in which numerous dogs were being kept. Investigators had determined there were many dogs (including newborn puppies), mostly rat terriers, chihuahuas and mixed breeds located on the property, but were surprised by the exact number located. In anticipation of needing assistance with medical treatment and rescue shelter placement, MCSO Animal Services staff enlisted and coordinated additional resources from Animal Rescue Corps, based in Washington, DC.
Upon arrival, the property owner, Matthew Donalies, was placed under arrest without incident. The investigation determined that Donalies had been operating a backyard breeding mill and had been selling dogs via the internet for several years. After securing the arrest, the rescue operation began. A large triage station was set up that included veterinary staff and members of the Animal Rescue Corps. The rescue operation lasted nearly 12 hours as the dogs were captured and removed from the property. A total of 146 dogs and one kitten were successfully rescued. Nearly every dog captured suffered from various illnesses and injuries including internal and external parasites, eye infections, abscessed teeth, overgrown nails and other untreated injuries.
All the dogs from this investigation were transported to ARC's Rescue Center, about 30 miles east of Nashville, Tenn. Each animal in this rescue operation will receive a thorough veterinary exam, appropriate vaccinations and necessary medical treatment, time to heal and recover before matched and transported to trusted shelters and rescue partner organizations that will ultimately adopt them into loving homes.
'Addressing animal cruelty and neglect is a responsibility we take with utmost seriousness, recognizing that animals are victims too,' said Sheriff Harper. 'I am extremely proud of my investigators and Animal Services staff for their hard work and dedication to the voiceless animals in Madison County each day. I am thankful for the support we receive from the community in our mission to address the uncared-for animal population. I am also very grateful to Animal Rescue Corps for providing the crucial resources necessary to ensure the safety of these animals and for supporting our community in protecting animals.'
Arrested:
Matthew Donalies
D.O.B. 08/10/1966
610 SE Askew Avenue
Madison, Fla.
1. Cruelty to Animals/Neglect Serious Injury or Death (142 counts)
F.S. 828.12.2
Since 2010, Animal Rescue Corps (ARC), a national animal protection nonprofit, has provided large-scale animal rescue for communities that lack resources to address abuse. In addition to emergency rescue, ARC offers education and shelter relief. ARC's mission is to end animal suffering through direct and compassionate action and to inspire the highest ethical standards of humanity toward animals. For more information about Animal Rescue Corps, visit animalrescuecorps.org.

title: Heath Driggers
description: Question 1. During the primary election only 33.3% of registered voters came out to vote. If elected, what initiatives will you promote to encourage civic engagement and higher turnout? Answer – As…
content:
Question 1. During the primary election only 33.3% of registered voters came out to vote. If elected, what initiatives will you promote to encourage civic engagement and higher turnout?
Answer – As your Supervisor of Elections, we prepare for a 100% turnout in every election in hopes that the voters of Madison County will show up and participate. It is extremely hard to reach all demographics with election messaging, however there is always room for improvement. Voter outreach is incredibly important, and we encourage an invitation to our office to allow us to participate in events happening within our community. More election ads in the local newspaper will assist with reaching our target audience. Creating a more robust social media platform is an area I would like to see improved. With social media software now available to assist with ad creation, a more engaging social media platform will assist your elections office with civic engagement which hopefully will lead to higher turnout.
Question 2. What strategies do you plan to implement if voted into office to educate voters about the voting process, including changes to laws, registration, and ballot measures?
Answer – The election laws are forever changing. Having served as your Supervisor of Elections for the last four years I have seen changes in every Florida Statute dealing with elections. Educating the voters of Madison County about election laws will absolutely tie back into civic engagement. Getting those messages out in a method that hopefully the voters will read is always a struggle. Educating the voters to know the difference between political mail and your Supervisor of Elections official election mail will be a top priority in differentiating the difference. Voters must also take responsibility to ask questions when unsure and ask those questions to their Supervisor of Elections office. We should always be your trusted source for election information.
Question 3. What is your vision for the Elections office over the next few years, and what key changes do you hope to implement if elected?
Answer – After every election, your Supervisor of Elections takes the time to reflect on what we feel like worked and what improvements can be made leading into the next election cycle. A few improvements that are already on my radar are: 1) Updating end of life servers and desktops. 2) Researching a new software platform called 'TextMyGov' which would give this office a more streamlined approach to a targeted group of individuals such as candidates, poll workers, and canvassing board members. It would also allow this office to mass text the voters within the county of upcoming deadlines and other important election information. Again, messaging is important for any election changes, civic engagement, and voter turnout. 3) Updating and implementing a stronger record retention policy. 4) Security is always a concern and researching what other layers of security might could be implemented would certainly benefit the voters of Madison County.

description: Leah Androski reporter@greenepublishing.com Madison County Central School (MCCS) will be holding a shoe donation drop-off to raise funds for their Lady Broncos Softball team from now until Saturday…
content:
Leah Androski
reporter@greenepublishing.com
Madison County Central School (MCCS) will be holding a shoe donation drop-off to raise funds for their Lady Broncos Softball team from now until Saturday, Feb. 8.
MCCS asks for any gently worn, used and new shoes to be donated. Shoes that have damaged or broken heels, soles or buckles, mismatched pairs or are wet or moldy will not be accepted. It is encouraged to not use any black, white or colored bags. MCCS also asks that you do not use rubber bands to close the bags of donated shoes.
When you donate shoes, MCCS asks that the shoes should be paired together with rubber rands or tied together by the laces. In every bag, there should be a max of 25 pairs of shoes, with the bag being tied shut. Only clear bags of shoes will be accepted. The shoes also need to be dry and clean. All shoes will be given to someone in need.
For any questions or for more information, please contact Coach Clayton McWilliams at (850) 464-2970.
